tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.

- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated
by Acacia verticillata (L'HCrit.) Willd.
at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria


David H. Ash ton and Jennifer A. Chappill
School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.




                                                                                                                Downloaded from connectsci.​au/​bt/​article-pdf/​37/​1/​1/​183149/​bt9890001.​pdf by UNSW Library user on 07 October 2026
Abstract
Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire Acacia verticillata scrub in areas originally supporting
sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The
potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, A. verticillata has been replaced
by drought-resistant Kunzea ambigua while o n wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant
Melaleuca ericifolia. In mid slopes A. verticillata is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer
of Pteridium esculentum and Goodenia ovata and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The compo-
sition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and
grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor
seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated
the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation
without the intervention of fire.




Introduction
   In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub
of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century
(Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the
fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus,
repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before
seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires
occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense
selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.
   The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is esti-
mated to be 95 km2 and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll
forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between
these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie et al.
(1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of Euca-
lyptus obliqua L'Htrit., E. muelleriana and E. regnans* have been destroyed in the last
60 years by numerous fires.
    Only 2.4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation
with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas
converted to scrub, about 68% (9.0 km2) are dominated by Acacia verticillata in damp
sclerophyll areas and 32% (4.3 km2) is dominated by Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia
arborescens, Olearia argophylla and 0.phlogopappa in the wetter areas. Although

=== PAGE 3
Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub

Fig. 2. The study site spur (L.H.S.) along Lilly Pilly valley looking towards Mt LaTrobe. (a) Dense
Acacia verticillata in flower October 1967; ( b ) Same site 1986 when the scrub community had
degenerated into a hummocky canopy of Melaleuca, Banksia and Kunzea; (c) Fenced and unfenced plots
at commencement of experiment in 1980.

cover apart from mosses, sparse Viola hederacea, occasional clumps Goodenia ovata
and rank Tetrarrhena juncea. After 10 years A . verticillata was mature and 4-5 m tall
(Fig. 2a), but after 20 years it had begun to senesce (Fig. 2b). Death of stands commenced on the lower slopes and warmer aspects and by 1979-80 most stands were dead
(Fig. 2c). The stems of the degenerating acacias were infested with numerous wood

The classification of the floristic composition of quadrats (10 by 2 m) produced six
groups (Fig. 4a) which could be interpreted in relation to topography. Although some
groups (I, V) comprised only quadrats from scrub vegetation (Table l), others (11) were
equally distributed between scrub and forest or indicated a distinct preference for one
or the other (VI, 111). The greatest number of species occurred in forested lower-mid
slopes (I), the lowest in wet scrub (IV). Most groups were characterised by gradations
of species frequencies although the predominant community in the mid-lower slopes of
Melaleuca-Kunzea-Banksia-Acacia was distinguished by the high frequency of Adianturn aethiopicum in the Pteridium-Goodenia field layer. The first two axes of the ordination of the groups (Fig. 4b) accounts for 60% of the quadrat variation. Axis 1
appears to be related loosely to topographic factors such as soil moisture gradients.


regularly measured. As the seedlings were not of a uniform age at the first measurement, the percentage

The vegetation cover and density in the fenced and unfenced plots was assessed by vertical point

counting numbers of individuals in 16 10 by 2 m quadrats in the lower mid-slope area in 1982 and 1983.
In early January 1980, five plots in the scrub, each 1 m2, were cleared of vegetation and litter with
minimal disturbance to the topsoil. In June, July and September of the same year the identifiable
seedlings in a central square, 30 by 30 cm, were counted and removed. In early February, soil was
collected from 10 random plots in the same community for examination of seed germination under more
favourable conditions of moisture and protection in seed trays placed in the open on a rooftop at the
University of Melbourne. Three depths of soil were sampled; 0-1 cm, 1-2 cm and 2-3 cm. The soil was
sieved and spread to a depth of 1 cm over sterile coarse sand in seed trays 28 by 32 cm. Germination
was monitored between March and July by counting seedlings and removing them as they were
identified.
In 1983, the relative frequency of herbivory o n various species was assessed in 16 10 by 2 m quadrats
o n the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub, each species being classified according to the relative
intensity of damage sustained (i, e. no damage, light, heavy). In the course of floristic assessment from
the ridge top to the swamp, faecal pellets within quadrats were counted and classified according to
species of origin.

# Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by *Acacia verticillata* (L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

## Abstract

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

## Introduction

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

## Materials and Methods

### Vegetation Structure and Composition

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

### Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub

An experimental plot 200 m² was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

## Abstract

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

## Introduction

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. ## Materials and Methods

### Vegetation Structure and Composition

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

### Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub

An experimental plot 200 m² was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

The vegetation cover and density in the fenced and unfenced plots was assessed by vertical point quadrats using pins 1·5 mm diameter and 2 m tall. These analyses were repeated at 1-2 year intervals from 1980 until 1986. The density of the major shrub species was also assessed outside the plots by counting numbers of individuals in 16 10 by 2 m quadrats in the lower mid-slope area in 1982 and 1983.

In early January 1980, five plots in the scrub, each 1 m², were cleared of vegetation and litter with minimal disturbance to the topsoil. In June, July and September of the same year the identifiable seedlings in a central square, 30 by 30 cm, were counted and removed. In early February, soil was collected from 10 random plots in the same community for examination of seed germination under more favourable conditions of moisture and protection in seed trays placed in the open on a rooftop at the University of Melbourne. Three depths of soil were sampled; 0-1 cm, 1-2 cm and 2-3 cm. The soil was sieved and spread to a depth of 1 cm over sterile coarse sand in seed trays 28 by 32 cm. Germination was monitored between March and July by counting seedlings and removing them as they were identified.

In 1983, the relative frequency of herbivory on various species was assessed in 16 10 by 2 m quadrats on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub, each species being classified according to the relative intensity of damage sustained (i. e. no damage, light, heavy). ## Results

### Vegetation Structure and Composition

The classification of the floristic composition of quadrats (10 by 2 m) produced six groups (Fig. 4*a*) which could be interpreted in relation to topography. Although some groups (I, V) comprised only quadrats from scrub vegetation (Table 1), others (II) were equally distributed between scrub and forest or indicated a distinct preference for one or the other (VI, III). The greatest number of species occurred in forested lower-mid slopes (I), the lowest in wet scrub (IV). Most groups were characterised by gradations of species frequencies although the predominant community in the mid-lower slopes of *Melaleuca-Kunzea-Banksia-Acacia* was distinguished by the high frequency of *Adiantum aethiopicum* in the *Pteridium-Goodenia* field layer. The first two axes of the ordination of the groups (Fig. 4*b*) accounts for 60% of the quadrat variation. Axis 1 appears to be related loosely to topographic factors such as soil moisture gradients.

No significant differences between species were observed. However, in 1986 the tallest of the dominant-crowned individuals of *E. muelleriana* (400 cm) far exceeded the tallest *E. obliqua* (256 cm) and *E. baxteri* (285 cm). A longer-term study may show that *E. muelleriana* will come to dominate the site in future years.

The effect of the fencing treatment was significant by April 1980, when all species showed greater height growth (at *P* = 0·05) in the fenced than unfenced plots. Height growth of the eucalypt species in the fenced plots increased markedly in the second and third years, in spite of the severe drought of 1982 (Fig. 8).

The difference in survival between different species of eucalypt during the 6 years of the study were marked. *E. muelleriana* showed consistently higher survival rates than the other species after the first year and *E. obliqua* had the fewest seedlings surviving. After 12 months, only about 20% of the unfenced plants had survived, and after 2 years one plant of *E. muelleriana* remained, and that specimen remained only for an

The pooled data for all species in fenced and unfenced plots are shown in Fig. 9. *E. obliqua* was more severely attacked by groups of sawfly larvae than the other species, and *E. muelleriana* maintained large and horizontally displayed juvenile foliage for at least the second growing season.

The fate of large eucalypt seedlings planted at random in thick scrub and ground stratum in the mid-slope area indicated that plants 1-2 m tall could be located, pulled down and severely browsed, most probably by wallabies. After 3 years, all plants had been destroyed, even those in thick regrowth of *M. ericifolia* and *G. ovata*. The last surviving plant, 2 m tall in 1985, had disappeared without trace 1 year later.

Seeds of the three eucalypt species sown outside fences in mid to late autumn, germinated within 2 weeks and reached the 2-leaf stage and heights of 2-8 cm by the following spring. By December, browsing was evident in four out of 21 plants. By the following autumn all plants had disappeared.

# Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by *Acacia verticillata* (L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

## Abstract

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

## Introduction

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. the data of all microhabitats because of the low survival in the lighter cover classes. Two-way analyses of variance were performed after logarithmic transformation of each set of measurements. === PAGE 11
Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub


Regeneration of A , verticillata and Other Species in the Scrub
The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger
herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect
in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, T. juncea
and the raspwort, Gonocarpus teucrioides. Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10).
P. esculentum behaved similarly to T. juncea, but G. ovata declined steadily as its
associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be
higher in the fenced plots, although Coprosma quadrifida did not conform, due to its
development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2).
Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20
species).
In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced
the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots T. juncea decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly
dominated by non-grazed P. esculentum and G. ovata and with scattered spiny bushes
of C. quadrifida and A. verticillata. K. ambigua and M. ericifolia which are increasing
in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by woodboring insects on the lower stems.
The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area
of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. M. ericifolia is regenerating
vigorously from root suckers and A. verticillata is also regenerating well from soil-stored
seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further
replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction
of height and density of A. verticillata in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.
The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given
in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from
the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per
square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in
the trays than in the field, with the exception of Hydrocotyle hirta and V. hederacea.
Some species such as Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata and Schoenus apogon
appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable
absence of T. juncea, may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since
this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell
1981).
The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis
indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores
and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect
the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980
within the fenced plots. Hog deer (Axis porcinus) are present in the area but d o not
appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.
It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area
have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both C. quadr$da and
A , verticillata are protected to some extent by spines, whilst G. ovata, K. ambigua and
M. ericifolia appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect
attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage
occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser
vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as V. hederacea, Stellaria flaccida and
G. teucrioides were severely grazed, but P. esculentum and G. ovata were conspicuously
undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

lines: +# Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by *Acacia verticillata* (L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria
+*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*
+School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.
+## Abstract

+Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia*. In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.
+## Introduction

+In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

+The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km² and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

+Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km²) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km²) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera*, *Bedfordia arborescens*, *Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. Acknowledgments
We thank Dr P . Y. Ladiges and an anonymous reviewer for criticising the manuscript, and ecology students of 1983 and 1986 for assistance in assessing vegetation and
plots. We gratefully acknowledge the permission given by the Victorian National Parks
Service to carry out this research, and for their help in erecting fenced plots. The

ance and longevity of other dominants such as B. marginata, C. quadrifida, K. ambigua
a n d M. ericifolia. The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny
a t shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to
avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially
dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals
of A. verticillata flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank
of this species.
The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically.
With the demise of the A. verticillata stratum the high percentage of bare ground was
subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The
patchy regeneration of A. verticillata, which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of P. esculentum and
G. ovata increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, A. verticillata
has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand
is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than
15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century
may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole
topographic range.
Only under very rare instances d o eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention
of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance
of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of Eucalyptus species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the
two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred
between the three contending species in the area - E. obliqua, E. muelleriana and
E. baxteri. When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant
ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources
for E, obliqua and E. rnuelleriana used.
In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite
for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5
tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be
expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in nonfire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant
eucalypt seed production.
The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would
require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be
an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from
which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance.
However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled
fire regimes.

dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals
of A. verticillata flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank
of this species.
The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically.
With the demise of the A. verticillata stratum the high percentage of bare ground was
subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The
patchy regeneration of A. verticillata, which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of P. esculentum and
G. ovata increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, A. verticillata
has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand
is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than
15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century
may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole
topographic range.
Only under very rare instances d o eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention
of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance
of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of Eucalyptus species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the
two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred
between the three contending species in the area - E. obliqua, E. muelleriana and
E. baxteri. When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant
ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources
for E, obliqua and E. rnuelleriana used.
In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite
for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5
tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be
expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in nonfire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant
eucalypt seed production.
The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would
require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be
an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from
which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance.
However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 11

### Regeneration of *A. verticillata* and Other Species in the Scrub

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides*. Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea*, but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata*. *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea*. Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa*, *Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea*, may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer (*Axis porcinus*) are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea*, *Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

## Discussion

Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. The development of sclerophyll open forests is the product of site quality and fire regime (Gill 1975). In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).

ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata*, *C. quadrifida*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia*. The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata*, which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area — *E. obliqua*, *E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri*. When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 11

### Regeneration of *A. verticillata* and Other Species in the Scrub

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides*. Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea*, but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata*. *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea*. Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa*, *Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea*, may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer (*Axis porcinus*) are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea*, *Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

## Discussion

Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. The development of sclerophyll open forests is the product of site quality and fire regime (Gill 1975). In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).

In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler-

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 17

ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata*, *C. quadrifida*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia*. The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata*, which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area — *E. obliqua*, *E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri*. When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

### Regeneration of *A. verticillata* and Other Species in the Scrub

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides*. Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea*, but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata*. *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea*. Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa*, *Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea*, may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer (*Axis porcinus*) are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea*, *Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).

In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler-

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 17

ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata*, *C. quadrifida*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia*. The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata*, which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area — *E. obliqua*, *E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri*. When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 11

### Regeneration of *A. verticillata* and Other Species in the Scrub

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides*. Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea*, but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata*. *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea*. Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa*, *Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea*, may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer (*Axis porcinus*) are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata*, *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea*, *Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

## Discussion

Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).
