+#### **Abstract**
+**Question:** What is the role of dispersal, persistent soil seed banks and seedling recruitment in population persistence of fleshy-fruited obligate seeding plant species in fire-prone habitats?
+**Location:** Southeastern Australia.

+**Methods:** We used a long-term study of a shrubby, fleshy-fruited *Persoonia* species (*Proteaceae*) to examine (1) seed removal from beneath the canopy of adult plants; (2) seedling recruitment after fire; (3) the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank; and (4) the implications for fire management of obligate seeding species. We used demographic sampling techniques combined with Generalised Linear Modelling and regression to quantify population changes over time.

+**Results:** Most of the mature fruits (90%) on the ground below the canopy of plants were removed by *Wallabia bicolor* (Swamp wallaby) with 88% of seeds extracted from *W. bicolor* scats viable and dormant. Wallabies play an important role in moving seeds away from parent plants. Their role in occasional long distance dispersal events remains unknown. We detected almost no seed predation *in situ* under canopies (< 1%). Seedling recruitment was cued to fire, with post-fire seedling densities 6-7 times pre-fire adult densities. After fire, a residual soil seed bank was present, as many seeds (77-100%) remained dormant and viable at a soil depth where successful future seedling emergence is possible (0-5 cm). Seedling survival was high (> 80%) with most mortality within 2 years of emergence. Plant growth averaged 17 cm per year. The primary juvenile period of plants was 7-8 years, within the period of likely return fire intervals in the study area. We predicted that the study population increased some five-fold after the wildfire at the site.

+**Conclusions**: Residual soil seed banks are important, especially in species with long primary juvenile periods, to buffer the populations against the impact of a second fire occurring before the seed bank is replenished.
+**Keywords:** Fire frequency; Macropod; Mammal; Obligate seeder; Soil seed bank.
+**Nomenclature:** Harden, G.J. (1990-1992).
+# **Dispersal and recruitment dynamics in the fleshy-fruited** *Persoonia lanceolata* **(Proteaceae)**
+**Auld, Tony D.**1\***; Denham, Andrew J.**1,2 **& Turner, Ken**<sup>3</sup>

+1*Biodiversity Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 1967, Hurstville NSW 2220 Australia;* 2*E-Mail andrew.denham@environment.nsw.gov.au;* 3*Native Vegetation Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 867 Wollongong, NSW 2520 Australia; E-mail ken.turner@dnr.nsw.gov.au \*Corresponding author; E-mail tony.auld@environment.nsw.gov.au*
+## **Introduction**

+Persistence of plant populations is influenced by a range of factors (Harper 1977). Ultimately, all plant populations rely on recruitment from seed to compensate for the death of individuals. For plants that occur in fireprone habitats and are killed by fire (obligate seeders), recruitment is often linked to the passage of fire (Keeley 1991; Tyler 1995; Whelan 1995). The abundance and distribution of new recruits in such plant populations is controlled by a combination of factors. These include: (1) amount of seed produced (e.g. Enright & Lamont 1989); (2) seed dispersal to safe sites (Hughes & Westoby 1992; Lamont et al. 1993); (3) factors that govern the breaking of seed dormancy and promote seed germination (Auld & O'Connell 1991; Baskin & Baskin 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Ooi et al. 2006); and (4) early seedling survival (Tyler 1995, 1996). As adults of obligate seeding species are killed by fire, sufficient time between fires is needed to replenish seed banks. Fire regimes that allow fires to repeatedly occur before seed banks are replenished may cause population declines or local extinction. Avoiding such fire regimes is necessary in order to manage fire-prone habitats for the conservation of biodiversity (Bradstock et al. 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Gill 2001; Keith et al. 2002; Whelan 2002). An understanding of the dynamics of seed dispersal and factors influencing recruitment is necessary to determine how obligate seeding species respond to changes in fire regimes that result from direct human activities and climate change (Whelan 1986).

+Seed dispersal of woody species in many fire-prone habitats can be limited, as indicated by the predominance of myrmecochory in SE and SW Australia (Berg 1975; Rice & Westoby 1981) and elsewhere (Gomez & Espadaler 1998). For such species, the capacity to reoccupy sites should a species be adversely affected by fire regimes is limited (Whelan 1986, 1995), especially where habitats are highly fragmented by urban and rural development. For some species, there is a greater
+{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+capacity for dispersal, through either wind dispersal of small seeds or dispersal by animal vectors. Fleshyfruited species that may be moved by vertebrates are a small component of the heath and woodland flora of southeastern Australia (French & Westoby 1996) and other fire-prone floras (Bullock 1978; Milewski & Bond 1981; Keeley 1991). This may be the result of the low soil fertility that characterises the vegetation in these areas (Westoby et al. 1990). We estimate, based on seed morphology characteristics, that in the Sydney region, only some 9 % of species (in 57 genera) that occur in fire-prone heaths, woodlands and dry forest habitats have fleshy fruits that are likely to be dispersed by vertebrates. The most abundant groups are from two diverse families, *Persoonia* in the Proteaceae (29 taxa) and *Acrotriche*, *Astroloma, Brachyloma*, *Leucopogon, Lissanthe, Melichrus*, *Monotoca* and *Styphelia* in the *Ericaceae* (formerly included in the Epacridaceae, 43 taxa). The role of seed dispersal in maintaining populations or in moving seeds between populations in such taxa is poorly known.

+*Persoonia* is an endemic Australian genus of ca. 100 species (Weston 2002), with two main centres of radiation, southeastern and southwestern Australia. Obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. may have long primary juvenile periods, relative to the average inter-fire interval (Benson 1985; Auld unpubl.) and a number are threatened in the Sydney Basin of southeastern Australia (Rymer 2006). Such species are at risk of decline if fire frequencies are increased via arson, climate change or burning for protection of life and property.

+In this paper we report on a long-term study of one obligate seeding shrub species, *Persoonia lanceolata*  Andrews, that is common in eastern Australia and is a significant structural component of vegetation in heaths and woodlands. We ask:
+- 1. Is seed removed or eaten from beneath the canopy of adult plants?
+- 2. What agents are involved in seed removal or seed predation?
+- 3. What is the magnitude of seedling recruitment after fire? Does this suggest population stability under the current fire regime?
+- 4. What is the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank? How is this related to the pre-fire seed density? and
+- 5. What are the implications for fire management of obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp.?
+## **Methods**
+#### *Study species and site*

+*Persoonia lanceolata* is a bushy shrub that grows to 3 m high. It is a fire sensitive obligate seeder, common in the understorey in heath and woodlands along the east coast and ranges of New South Wales, Australia (Weston 2002). Flowering occurs in summer (December to February) with mature fruits ripening in the following spring (September to October, Benson & McDougall 2000). The fruit of *Persoonia* species is a drupe (Weston 2002) of approximately 1300 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990), with a pulpy flesh surrounding a hard woody pyrene. There is mostly one seed per pyrene in *P. lanceolata* (Westoby et al. 1990; pers. obs.). Seed dispersal is thought to be mostly by mammals and birds (Benson & McDougall 2000).

+We examined a population of *P. lanceolata* at one site within Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park 20 km north of Sydney (33°53' E, 151°13' S) southeastern Australia. Annual precipitation for Sydney is around 1300 mm, while the average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures are 26/18 °C in summer and 16/8 °C in winter. The area of the site was ca. 2 ha and contained a dense mature population of *P. lanceolata* occurring in a periodically wet heathland. *Persoonia lanceolata* was one of the dominant shrubs along with *Angophora crassifolia*, *Eucalyptus stricta* and *Hakea teretifolia.*  There was a range of smaller shrub species (0.5 - 2 m), particularly members of the *Proteaceae* and *Fabaceae*  (common species include: *Banksia oblongifolia, Boronia pinnata, Dillwynia floribunda, Epacris pulchella, Grevillea speciosa, Hakea dactyloides, Leptospermum squarrosum, Mirbelia rubiifolia, Persoonia pinifolia, Pultenaea elliptica* and *Xanthorrhoea* spp.) and a ground cover of sedges, grasses, and herbs (common species include: *Actinotus minor, Anisopogon avenaceus, Bauera rubioides, Cyathochaeta diandra, Lindsaea linearis, Lomandra cylindrica, L. glauca, Mitrasacme polymorpha, Patersonia* sp.*, Restio* spec.). The site was burnt by an extensive summer (January) wildfire in 1994 that burnt all the surrounding habitat. It had previously been burnt in a summer wildfire 15 years prior.
+#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

+Prior to the wildfire, we established plots under randomly selected mature *P. lanceolata* plants over two consecutive fruiting seasons. In the first season, we established five plots in a pilot experiment that ran for 12 days. In the second season, we established ten plots and followed the fates of seeds for 40 days. At each plot we established two treatments;

+(1) a cache of 10 mature fruits; and (2) a cache of 10 mature fruits covered by a wire mesh cage (mesh 1 cm × 1 cm), cage 15 cm by 15 cm by 6 cm high. Each cage was placed over a petri dish and secured with wire stakes. These cages excluded vertebrates.

+All caches were placed in 9 cm diameter petri dishes to avoid fruits being washed away in storms. The fate of seeds in caches was checked twice daily for 4 days then daily for 10 days and then 2-3 times per week. Searches were made around the caches for fruits or fruit/seed remains if seeds were removed from the caches. Where mammals were suspected of taking seeds (where pieces of seed testa were found or whole seeds were removed overnight) additional trials were established to identify the likely animals responsible. Adhesive tape was placed on the edges of petri dishes containing seeds and hair samples of the mammal species removing seeds were collected. These animal hairs were identified by B. Triggs. Field trapping using Elliott type A aluminium folding box traps was conducted to determine which small mammal species were present at the site.

+A 2-factor GLIM was used to compare the proportion of caches where fruit were removed in the first 12 days in the caged and uncaged treatments, across two years (12 days being the length of time the experiment was run in the first season). A separate 1-factor GLIM examined the proportion of caches where fruit removal occurred across treatments at the end of the second season. In both cases a binomial error structure was used.

+We also searched the surrounding habitat for any scats that contained pyrenes or fruits. We collected numerous scats and removed the pyrenes from them. For 10 replicate samples of 10 pyrenes from these scats we estimated the non-dormant seed fraction by placing replicate batches of seeds into 9-cm diameter petri dishes on Whatmans Grade 1 filter paper at room temperatures. Distilled water was added to ensure the filter paper remained moist and germination was followed for 2 months after which seeds were extracted from pyrenes and tested for viability using tetrazolium (Lakon 1949).

+After the 1994 wildfire, we established 23 permanent 1-m2 quadrats within the population using a randomised grid. New seedlings (71) were identified by their distinctive cotyledons. At each sampling, we scored plant survivorship, assessed whether the plants had reached maturity (as indicated by the production of flowers and then fruits), and measured the height of all tagged *P. lan-* *ceolata* plants as an indicator of their growth to maturity. The time to first flowering was recorded for all seedlings and the magnitude of fruit production estimated in several flowering seasons by counting large (near mature) fruits on all tagged plants. The rate of growth of plants was examined using non-linear regression (power function) of plant height (lognormal transformed) against plant age. As plants were repeatedly sampled, we also carried out an Analysis of Covariance with previous sample plant height as a covariate. We also compared the pre-fire density of plants with the post-fire seedling density as an estimate of population turnover after the fire.
+#### *Residual soil seed bank*

+Within a randomly chosen subset (8) of the 23 available 1-m2 quadrats described above to follow seedling emergence, survival and growth, we examined the residual soil seed bank. In 2003, 9 years after the 1994 fire (after seedlings had had their first flowering, but before the first post-fire seed fall) we excavated the soil in each of the 8 (1-m2) plots. All the soil in each plot was excavated in two parts, i.e. 0 to 5 cm and 5-10 cm depths. Pyrenes were extracted by sieving. Samples were wet sieved by washing through firstly a 6.3 mm followed by a 4.2 mm sieve. The retained parts were allowed to dry and hand sorted. Pyrenes passed through the first sieve and were retained by the second. Intact pyrenes were opened to determine if the fruit contained a viable seed (filled, firm and white).
+## **Results**
+#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

+Seed removal outside cages after 12 days occurred in both sampled seasons (GLIM Δ dev = 14.1, 1 df, *P* < 0.005), with no interaction between years and treatment (GLIM Δ dev = 0.0, 1 df, *P* > 0.05) and no year effect (GLIM Δ dev = 0.1, 1 df, *P* > 0.05). Averaged across the two years some 17% of seed was removed (removal occurring in 53 % of seed caches) in 12 days (Fig. 1). At the end of the second sample season, where we followed the fate of seeds for 40 days, the treatment effect was again significant (GLIM Δ dev = 16.9, 1 df, *P <* 0.005), with an average of 90% of fruits removed in the open (removal occurring in 100 % of seed caches). The rate of seed removal outside the cages was slow but continued over the 40 day trial (Fig. 1). Inside cages, there was occasional consumption of the flesh around pyrenes, and occasionally whole fruits were removed. Outside of cages most losses were fruit removals, although in a very few cases the pyrene was removed and the flesh remained.
+{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+#### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire*

+Most seedlings emerged in the first 10 months after the 1994 fire (the time of our first sample). There was only limited emergence after this (Table 1), but occasional seedlings appeared until 6 years post-fire. This subsequent emergence was not confined to any particular season (summer 11, autumn 6, winter 3 seedlings, respectively), and declined in magnitude over time. Seedling survival was high with most observed mortality in the first 1-2 years after seedlings were tagged (Fig. 2). Our sampling did not allow us to detect mortality in the first 10 months post-fire. The post-fire seedling density was 6-7 times greater than the pre-fire adult density (0.5 vs. 3.3/m2).
+Seedlings reached a height of ca. 1 m (range 0.10 - 1.7m) at 6-7 years old, growing at an average rate of 0.17m per year (Fig. 3). Age was a good predictor of plant

+Only two fruits in the experiment in the first year were observed to have been eaten *in situ*. Where whole seed removals occurred, two lines of evidence suggested that the fruits were eaten by the macropod *Wallabia bicolor* (swamp wallaby). Hair samples from around batches of seeds were identified as this species and scats of the species frequently contained *Persoonia* pyrenes. Field trapping of small mammals using Elliott Traps showed that only *Rattus fuscipes* and *Antechinus* sp. (a marsupial mouse) were commonly trapped at the site. Neither species is known to remove large fleshy fruits.
+For the pyrenes extracted from *Wallabia bicolor*  (Swamp Wallaby) scats we found high seed viability (88 ± 3%), but all viable seeds were still dormant.

+height with a power function of log height accounting for some 87% of the variation in mean plant height. The Analysis of Covariance showed a significant effect of both plant age (*P* < 0.001) and previous plant height (*P* < 0.001), suggesting that although a number of smaller plants persist for a while (see Fig. 3), the height of a plant at a particular age was not simply dependent on its previous height.

+No plants flowered until 6 years after the fire. At this time only 13% of plants were mature and resultant fruit production was very low (Table 1). The proportion of plants that reproduced increased over time up to 92% 12 years after the fire. The magnitude of fruit production also increased markedly from the first to the second fruiting season and in subsequent seasons (Table 1).
+#### *Residual soil seed bank*

+Residual seeds in the soil were found in all sampled quadrats, independent of whether or not above ground seedlings were present at the time of sampling (Fig. 4). The density of seeds in the soil (21.2 ± 5.1 seeds/m2) was some 6-7 times greater than the density of seedlings that emerged after fire. On a 1-m2 plot basis, we estimate that between 72-100% of the available soil seed bank did not germinate after the wildfire. This may be an overestimate, as some seeds that germinated may not have been observed as seedlings at our first census 10 months after the fire. Most of the residual soil seed bank was in the top 5 cm of soil (90%).
+## **Discussion**

+Fire plays an important part in the life cycle of many plant species, including woody *Persoonia* species. Like many other obligate seeders, for the common *P. lanceolata*, fire caused population-scale adult mortality and promoted the recruitment of new plants. Population persistence in this obligate seeding species will be influenced by fire frequency, fire patchiness and the dispersal capability of seeds. After a single fire, most seedling recruitment was confined to the first 1-2 years, suggesting that seeds of this species respond to fire cues and/or that the post-fire environment provides favourable conditions for seedling establishment. For obligate seeding shrubs in general, recruitment is often linked to the first 12 months after fire, e.g. southeastern Australia (Purdie 1977; Auld & Tozer 1995; Benwell 1998); Spanish matorral (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994); Florida sand pine scrub (Carrington 1999); Californian chaparral and sage brush (Keeley et al. 2006). However, there was no seasonal component observed in seedling emergence after the initial flush (in comparison to Auld et al. 2000; Ooi et al. 2004). Some continued seedling recruitment occurred for up to 6 years post-fire.

+The number of seedlings recruited post-fire exceeded pre-fire adult numbers by 6-7 times. The likely change in population abundance after the wildfire can be compared using an estimate of pre-fire adults to post-fire seedlings, and incorporating estimated subsequent seedling mortality levels. This included mortality prior to plants reaching maturity (Fig. 2, ca. 14 (± 4)% after 7.5 years) and an estimate of the likely subsequent adult mortality in the following 7.5 years (to allow equivalent populations estimates for a 15-year old stand). We assumed mortality from 7.5-15 years post-fire matched that of the 2-12 year old plants in the study (Fig. 2). Based on these estimates, we predict that the population density 15 years after the

+**Fig. 4.** Magnitude of the residual soil seed bank in *Persoonia lanceolata* in 1-m2 quadrats.
+{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+1994 wildfire would be some 5 × that of the pre-fire density. Few comparable examples of quantitative estimates of population change in response to fire are available. Keeley et al. (2006) observed an increase in abundance in obligate seeding shrubs in the first five years postfire in southern California, whilst Auld & Scott (2004) showed that the ratio of pre vs. post-fire plant abundance in obligate seeders was dependent upon the time since the previous fire (i.e. pre-fire plant ages). This general lack of data in fire-prone habitats limits quantitative comparison of the impact of varying fire regimes on persistence of obligate seeding plants.

+Survival of new seedlings of *P. lanceolata* is of a Deevey Type III (*sensu* Harper 1977), with highest mortality when plants are young and small, and reduced mortality once the seedlings are established and grow. This matches the pattern for seedlings in other fireprone habitats (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994; Whelan 1995). Plant growth is relatively slow compared to co-habiting obligate seeding shrubs and in this study, flowering did not occur until 6 years after the fire. As it takes over 6 months for fruits to mature and as the first flowering effectively produced almost no seed, we consider the first effective fruit set was some 7-8 years after the fire. This relatively long primary juvenile period has been noted at other sites for this species (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.), although it has also been observed to be slightly shorter (Benson & McDougall 2000). It is also typical of other co-habiting, obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. such as *P. pinifolia* and *P. isophylla* (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.). Fires may readily re-occur in the habitat of *P. lanceolata* every 5-10 years, with most (75%) areas in nearby comparable vegetation having a current fire return interval of 7-17 years (Bradstock & Kenny 2003). Consequently, the species may be at risk of population declines unless either a significant proportion of the soil seed bank remains available after a fire (as a residual seed bank), or seeds can readily disperse back into the population from unburnt populations.

+We found considerable residual seed at our study site and much of this lay in the top 5 cm of the soil, the area most likely to be influenced by fire-related germination cues such as heat (Bradstock & Auld 1995), and possibly smoke. These buried seeds are unlikely to be killed by the lethal heating effects of a fire. Seeds in the top 5 cm will also be least affected by limitations to successful emergence due to depth constraints (Bond et al. 1999). Residual seed values varied, but all greatly exceeded those of some other obligate seeders that co-occur with *P. lanceolata* (Auld & Denham 2006). However, even the residual soil seed bank detected in this study does not ensure there will be population level replacement should a fire occur before there has been replenishment of the soil seed bank. The magnitude of any germination event will be governed by factors relating to the fire itself (heat and smoke output) and post-fire rainfall levels.

+Removal of fruits from below parent shrubs by Swamp Wallabies was common. In contrast, removal by invertebrates was uncommon, as observed for this species at other sites by French & Westoby (1996). Very few seeds were consumed below canopies. In contrast to some other members of the *Proteaceae* such as *Grevillea* (Auld & Denham 1999), seed removal does not seem to be a mechanism for seed escape from seed predators. Rather, seed removal by Swamp Wallabies would likely reduce future seedling densities adjacent to pre-fire parent plants. Seeds that were removed passed though the gut of animals in a viable and dormant state. Hence, Swamp Wallabies are likely to be an effective dispersal agent for *Persoonia* spp., in agreement with Rymer (2006). Most seeds are likely to be deposited within a population, as evidenced by numerous scats containing seeds in the population. The question remains as to whether these dispersal agents have the ability to move seeds between populations, especially in order to prevent local population extinctions under a regime of too frequent fire. It has been suggested that vertebrate dispersal of *Persoonia* seeds may be a mechanism for gene flow between populations (Rymer & Ayre 2006) or for re-establishment of populations after local extinction (French & Westoby 1996).

+The long-term nature of this study allowed us to quantify population processes and changes over time. Such studies are a trade off between parameter estimation and predictability across the landscape (Silvertown & Lovett Doust 1983; Whelan 1995). The utility of these data for making predictions about other populations of *Persoonia lanceolata* remains to be investigated.
+## **Conclusions**

+The observed maintenance of a large post-fire residual soil seed bank was potentially an effective means of buffering the population from local extinction if fires occasionally re-occur at short intervals. A long-term high frequency fire regime that prevents the replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to lead to population declines and possible local extinction. We suggest that a sound understanding of how fire impacts on obligate seeding species, such as *Persoonia,* will be best developed by a combination of long-term studies at particular sites combined with detailed multi-site or multi-species comparisons of key demographic attributes, e.g. seed germination, seed dispersal patterns, residual soil seed banks.

Adults in the second group are fire-sensitive and generally killed outright (Gill, 1975, 1981; Bradstock, 1981). The relative proportions of these groups of species appear to be related to the fire frequency in the habitat (Christensen, Recher & Hoare, 1981). In wet sclerophyll forest the proportion of fire-sensitive species is roughly 50 to 60 per cent (Ashton, 1981). In the more frequently burnt dry sclerophyll forests near Canberra, Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found 65 per cent regenerated vegetatively but only 27 per cent of species were fire-sensitive and only regenerated from seed. The time necessary for reproduction after fire is an important characteristic, especially in fire-sensitive species. Specht, Rayson & Jackman (1958) noted that fires at intervals of five years in heath vegetation are likely to eliminate or reduce numbers of some species that take several years to reach reproductive maturity. Similarly, for bushland north of Sydney, Siddiqi, Carolin & Myerscough (1976) recorded the localized elimination of the woody fire-sensitive species Banksia ericifolia, Allocasuarina distyla and Hakea teretifolia by repeated burning. However, to predict the impact of a series of fires, data on the maturation periods for fire-sensitive species are needed. With some exceptions, e.g. Banksia ericifolia (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) and Leptospermum laevigatum (Burrell, 1968), such data are not available. The potential effect of frequent burning on fire-sensitive species has become particularly relevant with the increased adoption of “controlled” or “prescribed” burning in bushland areas. Such burning generally involves the application of regular fires of low intensity, commonly at intervals of between two and five years. This paper documents the time required for a group of fire-sensitive species to reach maturity and discusses the implications for regular, frequent burning programs. 340 Cunninghamia Vol. 1{3): 1985 ##### METHODS The main study locality was in Brisbane Water National Park (33° 30'S, 151° 15'E), 40 km north of Sydney. Bushland here is eucalypt-dominated scleromorphic vegetation on low-nutrient Hawkesbury Sandstone. Rainfall is about 1250 mm per annum (Bureau of Meteorology, 1979). The general vegetation is described by Benson & Fallding (1981). A second locality was studied at Glenorie (33° 35’S, 151° 00'B), 15 km north-west of Hornsby, on similar Hawkesbury Sandstone, but with average rainfall of 930 mm per annum, to see whether similar results were obtained in a lower rainfall. A hot summer (1974-75) fire occurred at the Brisbane Water locality six months before the first observations were made and the size of dead bushes at the time indicated that the area had been unburnt for about 15 years before this. Fruit set occurred in most species. An exception was Grevillea sericea in which marked plants failed to set fruit after first flowering, but did so after subsequent flowering. In many species, notably those of the family Rutaceae, seed is released within a few months of flowering, but some species, particularly those of the woodyfruited Proteaceae, take a year after flowering for the characteristic woody follicles to develop. Examples are Banksia ericifolia, Hakea teretifolia and Petrophile pulchella, the slowest to flower of the species in the study area. A decline in numbers following flowering was recorded for Mitrasacme polymorpha, Poranthera ericifolia and in particular Actinotus helianthi. Individuals of these species had completely disappeared within five years; they may be regarded as early successional species. No further species disappeared from the plots during the recording period except for a number of species represented by only a single marked individual. 345 — rr ——————————————————— ccc, Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species The recorded times to achieve flowering for plants in the vicinity (Table 2) are almost all much shorter than for the marked plants, but do not really indicate the responses of the population as a whole. This is because many recordings are of individuals that were either unaffected or only slightly affected by the fire, as a result of the protection offered by the minor cliff-line, rock-outcrop and moist-soak microhabitats. The results indicate the potential resilience of a system in which considerable topographic variation provides fire refugia, but cannot be extrapolated to sites with less variable topography. The effect of the low intensity fire at site A was interesting — Poranthera ericifolia and Gonocarpus teucrioides, which had died out before the fire, reappeared. However, individuals of Platysace linearifolia, which had appeared only as seedlings after the 1974-75 summer fire, were not killed but resprouted at ground level, indicating that fire-sensitivity in that species may be related to the intensity of the fire. ###### DISCUSSION Fire-sensitive species may make up a significant component of Australian vegetation. For example, in dry sclerophyll communities near Canberra, of 93 species studied by Purdie & Slatyer (1976), 27 per cent were killed by fire and regenerated only from seed. A similar proportion are present in the scleromorphic flora of Sydney’s Hawkesbury Sandstone, particularly on the higher rainfall coastal areas. Of the species recorded in this study 20 are known to be fire-sensitive, and a further 13 are probably so. The only resprouter species to be marked were Actinotus minor, Platysace linearifolia, Banksia oblongifolia and B. serrata (neither of the marked Banksia species flowered during the recording period). Fire-sensitive species are likely to be severely disadvantaged and possibly eliminated by a series of fires at intervals less than the time taken for seedling regeneration to produce further seed. The results here show that fire-sensitive species may not flower for two to eight years after a fire. Major flowering is not attained for one or two years after that. Similar results were found for all sites at Brisbane Water and also at Glenorie, and are likely to apply to other areas on Sydney’s Hawkesbury Sandstone. The results highlight the variability present within most wild populations. For instance, although most individuals may flower simultaneously, there will generally be some individuals flowering out of season. Flowering is an effective indicator of maturity only if it is associated with the development of mature viable seed and leads to the build-up of an adequate seedbank. Some species, particularly those with woody fruits, take up to a year for the fruits to mature, and are vulnerable to fire during this period. Examples are Banksia ericifolia, Hakea teretifolia and Petrophile pulchella. Although fruit formation generally appears to accompany flowering, the percentage viability of the first seeds set by an individual may not be known. In B. ericifolia, B. serrata, P. pulchella and Isopogon anemonifolius, first seed set on juvenile plants is normal in terms of viability, i.e. it is comparable to seed viability produced in older plants. However, the number of seeds per cone is often significantly lower in the first and second crops (R. Bradstock, pers. comm.). The density of seedlings at the beginning of this work and the early seedling mortality encountered suggest that some species recruit from a relatively large seedbank either already stored in the soil or available from woody capsules. Certainly, for the survival of each species a minimum seedbank must be present, though the necessary size for most species is unknown. 346 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985 Without this seedbank, floristic composition will change to a dominance by resprouter or rhizomatous species, or to annual species, commonly exotics, which seed rapidly. Though rhizomatous species such as Pteridium esculentum and monocotyledonous families such as Poaceae and Cyperaceae can spread vegetatively, most dicotyledonous resprouters, with the exception of some which root-sucker, cannot and so rely on seed for the establishment of new individuals. Frequent burning may possibly weaken and eventually kill individual resprouters, so that some seedling establishment is necessary to replace them if the plant community composition is to remain reasonably stable. The critical fire-free period here will be the interval from seedling establishment to the production of an adequate fireresistant rootstock. However, since seedling recruitment will not be necessary after every fire, the critical fire-free period will not be needed for every fire cycle. Almost all seedlings appear to establish in the first two years after fire, when there is considerable seedling mortality. Similar results were recorded by Purdie (1977) for dry sclerophyll vegetation near Canberra. After this period, with the exception of a few short-lived species (e.g. Actinotus helianthi), few of the marked plants died, despite very dry conditions during the latter part of the recording period. Eight years after fire the shrub component of the plant community appears healthy and actively growing, with no sign of senescence. It is likely that such conditions will continue for 15 to 20 years after fire. The localized elimination of the tall woody species Banksia ericifolia, Allocasuarina distyla and Hakea teretifolia by frequent repeated burning has been reported at North Head, Sydney (Siddiqi et al, 1976). Generally, however, the local disappearance of species in bushland has not been recorded. If there has indeed been a loss, the absence of observations could be for two reasons. Firstly, the physiographic and habitat variation within the Hawkesbury Sandstone environment provides an uneven burn pattern with varying local fire intensities and localized fire refuges such as around rocky outcrops, cliff-lines or moist gullies. Our records of flowering within a year of the 1974-75 fire by the fire-sensitive species Boronia serrulata, Eriostemon buxifolius and E. australasius were from unburnt individuals growing amongst rock outcrops, which had ‘provided fire protection. Thus, a plant community may be able to recover from potentially disastrous too-frequent burns by re-invasion from unburnt refuges. However, a succession of frequent burns will greatly increase the chances of losing species. Secondly, the impressive species richness and diversity of plant communities on Hawkesbury Sandstone (426 dicotyledons are recorded for Brisbane Water National Park by Benson & Fallding, 1981) obscures, for most casual observers, changes in the abundance of individual species, particularly the less abundant and less conspicuous species, and particularly where such changes may be taking place gradually over decades. Most of the literature on the effect of fires on fire-sensitive species in the Sydney area concerns Banksia ericifolia, one of the most conspicuous and abundant species (e.g. Carpenter & Recher, 1979; Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981). Indeed, it may be the less common species that are more likely to be endangered by toofrequent fires. In their list of rare and restricted species in Brisbane Water National Park, Benson & Fallding (1981) include a number that are probably fire-sensitive. These include Leucopogon amplexicaulis, found in areas with low fire frequency, L. margarodes in areas not burnt for eight to ten years, Darwinia procera on a rocky ridge, and D. glaucophylla on rock outcrops that evidently protect it from fire, but it is not known whether these have previously been more abundant and whether frequent burning has endangered them. 347 ## EE # ——————————E—EEESEEEEeEE SSCS Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species #### FIRE MANAGEMENT IN NATURAL AREAS The effects of frequent burning in bushland areas have become particularly important with the increasing use of regular burning as a management tool. Such burning may be “controlled” (and intended only for fuel reduction) or “prescribed” (and sometimes involve biological as well as fuel reduction aims). Both involve the application of regular low-intensity fires, generally at intervals of between two and five years, though planned frequencies often vary widely in reality, to reduce flammable fuel. This is most commonly carried out during cool weather in autumn or spring, in order to keep fire intensities low and manageable. High-intensity prescribed burning is theoretically possible and may be biologically desirable, but there are problems with implementation (for details see Good, 1981, Luke & McArthur, 1978; Foster, 1976). The use of control burning at these frequencies may have the following deleterious effects, which will be particularly undesirable in areas reserved for the protection of native plants. (1) Fire-sensitive species may be eliminated by repeated burning at time intervals that are less than that required to produce seed. For example, burning an area several times in quick succession is reported by Luke & McArthur (1978) to eliminate species of Acacia by exhausting their seedbank without allowing it to be replaced. (2) Fruiting in both fire-sensitive and fire-resistant species may be reduced by burning when the plants are in flower or have immature fruits. Though there will generally be some species in flower at any time of the year, many species have a concentrated peak in spring (Timms, 1978), followed by seed maturation and release in summer. This is common in the families Fabaceae and Rutaceae, which are particularly conspicuous in the Hawkesbury Sandstone flora. Thus, a season’s potential seed supply may be destroyed by burning when it is immature. (3) Fire-resistant species may be eliminated by continual weakening and death of individuals. For example, Noble (1982) reports that in western New South Wales, mallee eucalypts, generally regarded as having a marked tolerance to periodic fire through their ability to produce epicormic shoots, do die when burnt more than once, especially when one burn closely follows another. (4) Low-intensity fires may not stimulate adequate seedling germination, though allowing rhizomatous regeneration. Gill (1975) noted that for the Australian flora a high burning frequency often leads to dominance by monocotyledonous and fern species in place of shrubs. For example, Bradley (1972) reports on the occurrence of Pteridium esculentum and Culcita dubia after cool burns in Sydney bushland, while Luke & McArthur (1978) refer to /mperata cylindrica as prominent in coastal forests of northern New South Wales that have been burnt extensively. A likely result of these factors is that areas of bush may be simplified both floristically and structurally. For the fire-sensitive species examined, a period of six to seven years is needed to reach regular flowering. In addition, another year is required by some of the slowestflowering species to develop mature seed. The question of the time needed to establish adequate seedbank reserves, either in the soil or within the plant canopy, has not been determined for many species. It is likely that most species require several seed-bearing seasons for this. Thus, for the communities examined a minimum firefree period of nine to ten years is needed in a majority of fire cycles. An occasional burn followed quickly by another may be tolerated as seed reserves in the soil may 348 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985 not necessarily be exhausted by one fire. However, this is dependent on an adequate seedbank having been built up prior to the first fire. The implications for fire management in natural areas are obvious. Before a long-term burning regime is imposed on an area of native bushland, the consequences of that action should be evaluated. As far as the survival of plant species is concerned, where there are often very little reliable data, it is necessary to err on the conservative side. That is, the time intervals between burns, in a majority of fire cycles, should be longer than the minimum suggested by the present findings. ###### ACKNOWLEDGMENTS This paper would not have been possible but for the enthusiasm and dedication of Dorothy Darvodelsky, Avril Donovan, Florence Dwight, Marie and John Glass, Marge Gowan, Valerie Jones, Clarice Morris and Peter Price, who germinated interest in the work and have continued with the data collection every three months, in all weathers. BENSON (Accepted for publication 11.5.1984) 10 11 ABSTRACT 12 13 Benson, D. H. (National Herbarium of New South Wales, Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia 2000) 1985. Maturation periods for fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation. Cunninghamia_1(3), 339-349, The maturation times (period from germination to flowering) for a number of fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation at sites in Brisbane Water National Park and at Glenorie near Sydney were recorded from marked seedlings established after hot fires. They range from two to seven years for different species. The implications for fire management, particularly for controlled burning, are discussed. A fire-{ree period of at least nine to ten years is recommended for similar vegetation if successful flowering and seed set, and continued species survival is to occur. 14 15 ##### INTRODUCTION 16 17 Plant species fall into two main groups with regard to their response to fire: some are characterized by vegetative regrowth, where individuals either resprout from epicormic shoots on the trunk and major surviving limbs or, following the death of all above-ground stems, resprout from underground rootstocks, lignotubers or rhizomes (sprouters); others regenerate from seed either stored in the soil before the fire, carried on the plants in woody fruits and released after the fire, or carried in from adjacent unburnt areas (non-sprouters). Adults in the second group are fire-sensitive and generally killed outright (Gill, 1975, 1981; Bradstock, 1981). 18 19 The relative proportions of these groups of species appear to be related to the fire frequency in the habitat (Christensen, Recher & Hoare, 1981). In wet sclerophyll forest the proportion of fire-sensitive species is roughly 50 to 60 per cent (Ashton, 1981). In the more frequently burnt dry sclerophyll forests near Canberra, Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found 65 per cent regenerated vegetatively but only 27 per cent of species were fire-sensitive and only regenerated from seed. 20 21 The time necessary for reproduction after fire is an important characteristic, especially in fire-sensitive species. Specht, Rayson & Jackman (1958) noted that fires at intervals of five years in heath vegetation are likely to eliminate or reduce numbers of some species that take several years to reach reproductive maturity. Similarly, for bushland north of Sydney, Siddiqi, Carolin & Myerscough (1976) recorded the localized elimination of the woody fire-sensitive species Banksia ericifolia, Allocasuarina distyla and Hakea teretifolia by repeated burning. However, to predict the impact of a series of fires, data on the maturation periods for fire-sensitive species are needed. With some exceptions, e.g. Banksia ericifolia (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) and Leptospermum laevigatum (Burrell, 1968), such data are not available. The potential effect of frequent burning on fire-sensitive species has become particularly relevant with the increased adoption of “controlled” or “prescribed” burning in bushland areas. Such burning generally involves the application of regular fires of low intensity, commonly at intervals of between two and five years. 22 23 This paper documents the time required for a group of fire-sensitive species to reach maturity and discusses the implications for regular, frequent burning programs. 24 25 340 26 27 Cunninghamia 28 29 Vol. 1{3): 1985 30 31 ##### METHODS 32 33 The main study locality was in Brisbane Water National Park (33° 30'S, 151° 15'E), 40 km north of Sydney. Bushland here is eucalypt-dominated scleromorphic vegetation on low-nutrient Hawkesbury Sandstone. Rainfall is about 1250 mm per annum (Bureau of Meteorology, 1979). The general vegetation is described by Benson & Fallding (1981). 181 182 Fruit set occurred in most species. An exception was Grevillea sericea in which marked plants failed to set fruit after first flowering, but did so after subsequent flowering. In many species, notably those of the family Rutaceae, seed is released within a few months of flowering, but some species, particularly those of the woodyfruited Proteaceae, take a year after flowering for the characteristic woody follicles to develop. Examples are Banksia ericifolia, Hakea teretifolia and Petrophile pulchella, the slowest to flower of the species in the study area. 183 184 A decline in numbers following flowering was recorded for Mitrasacme polymorpha, Poranthera ericifolia and in particular Actinotus helianthi. Individuals of these species had completely disappeared within five years; they may be regarded as early successional species. No further species disappeared from the plots during the recording period except for a number of species represented by only a single marked individual. 185 186 345 187 188 — rr 189 190 ——————————————————— ccc, 191 192 Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 193 194 The recorded times to achieve flowering for plants in the vicinity (Table 2) are almost all much shorter than for the marked plants, but do not really indicate the responses of the population as a whole. This is because many recordings are of individuals that were either unaffected or only slightly affected by the fire, as a result of the protection offered by the minor cliff-line, rock-outcrop and moist-soak microhabitats. The results indicate the potential resilience of a system in which considerable topographic variation provides fire refugia, but cannot be extrapolated to sites with less variable topography. 195 196 The effect of the low intensity fire at site A was interesting — Poranthera ericifolia and Gonocarpus teucrioides, which had died out before the fire, reappeared. However, individuals of Platysace linearifolia, which had appeared only as seedlings after the 1974-75 summer fire, were not killed but resprouted at ground level, indicating that fire-sensitivity in that species may be related to the intensity of the fire. 197 198 ###### DISCUSSION 199 200 Fire-sensitive species may make up a significant component of Australian vegetation. For example, in dry sclerophyll communities near Canberra, of 93 species studied by Purdie & Slatyer (1976), 27 per cent were killed by fire and regenerated only from seed. A similar proportion are present in the scleromorphic flora of Sydney’s Hawkesbury Sandstone, particularly on the higher rainfall coastal areas. Of the species recorded in this study 20 are known to be fire-sensitive, and a further 13 are probably so. The only resprouter species to be marked were Actinotus minor, Platysace linearifolia, Banksia oblongifolia and B. serrata (neither of the marked Banksia species flowered during the recording period). Fire-sensitive species are likely to be severely disadvantaged and possibly eliminated by a series of fires at intervals less than the time taken for seedling regeneration to produce further seed. The results here show that fire-sensitive species may not flower for two to eight years after a fire. Major flowering is not attained for one or two years after that. Similar results were found for all sites at Brisbane Water and also at Glenorie, and are likely to apply to other areas on Sydney’s Hawkesbury Sandstone. 201 202 The results highlight the variability present within most wild populations. For instance, although most individuals may flower simultaneously, there will generally be some individuals flowering out of season. 203 204 Flowering is an effective indicator of maturity only if it is associated with the development of mature viable seed and leads to the build-up of an adequate seedbank. Some species, particularly those with woody fruits, take up to a year for the fruits to mature, and are vulnerable to fire during this period. Examples are Banksia ericifolia, Hakea teretifolia and Petrophile pulchella. Although fruit formation generally appears to accompany flowering, the percentage viability of the first seeds set by an individual may not be known. In B. ericifolia, B. serrata, P. pulchella and Isopogon anemonifolius, first seed set on juvenile plants is normal in terms of viability, i.e. it is comparable to seed viability produced in older plants. However, the number of seeds per cone is often significantly lower in the first and second crops (R. Bradstock, pers. comm.). The density of seedlings at the beginning of this work and the early seedling mortality encountered suggest that some species recruit from a relatively large seedbank either already stored in the soil or available from woody capsules. Certainly, for the survival of each species a minimum seedbank must be present, though the necessary size for most species is unknown. 205 206 346 207 208 Cunninghamia 209 210 Vol. 1(3): 1985 211 212 Without this seedbank, floristic composition will change to a dominance by resprouter or rhizomatous species, or to annual species, commonly exotics, which seed rapidly. Though rhizomatous species such as Pteridium esculentum and monocotyledonous families such as Poaceae and Cyperaceae can spread vegetatively, most dicotyledonous resprouters, with the exception of some which root-sucker, cannot and so rely on seed for the establishment of new individuals. Frequent burning may possibly weaken and eventually kill individual resprouters, so that some seedling establishment is necessary to replace them if the plant community composition is to remain reasonably stable. The critical fire-free period here will be the interval from seedling establishment to the production of an adequate fireresistant rootstock. However, since seedling recruitment will not be necessary after every fire, the critical fire-free period will not be needed for every fire cycle. 213 214 Almost all seedlings appear to establish in the first two years after fire, when there is considerable seedling mortality. Similar results were recorded by Purdie (1977) for dry sclerophyll vegetation near Canberra. After this period, with the exception of a few short-lived species (e.g. Actinotus helianthi), few of the marked plants died, despite very dry conditions during the latter part of the recording period. Eight years after fire the shrub component of the plant community appears healthy and actively growing, with no sign of senescence. It is likely that such conditions will continue for 15 to 20 years after fire. 215 216 The localized elimination of the tall woody species Banksia ericifolia, Allocasuarina distyla and Hakea teretifolia by frequent repeated burning has been reported at North Head, Sydney (Siddiqi et al, 1976). Generally, however, the local disappearance of species in bushland has not been recorded. If there has indeed been a loss, the absence of observations could be for two reasons. Firstly, the physiographic and habitat variation within the Hawkesbury Sandstone environment provides an uneven burn pattern with varying local fire intensities and localized fire refuges such as around rocky outcrops, cliff-lines or moist gullies. Our records of flowering within a year of the 1974-75 fire by the fire-sensitive species Boronia serrulata, Eriostemon buxifolius and E. australasius were from unburnt individuals growing amongst rock outcrops, which had ‘provided fire protection. Thus, a plant community may be able to recover from potentially disastrous too-frequent burns by re-invasion from unburnt refuges. However, a succession of frequent burns will greatly increase the chances of losing species. 217 218 Secondly, the impressive species richness and diversity of plant communities on Hawkesbury Sandstone (426 dicotyledons are recorded for Brisbane Water National Park by Benson & Fallding, 1981) obscures, for most casual observers, changes in the abundance of individual species, particularly the less abundant and less conspicuous species, and particularly where such changes may be taking place gradually over decades. Most of the literature on the effect of fires on fire-sensitive species in the Sydney area concerns Banksia ericifolia, one of the most conspicuous and abundant species (e.g. Carpenter & Recher, 1979; Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981). Indeed, it may be the less common species that are more likely to be endangered by toofrequent fires. In their list of rare and restricted species in Brisbane Water National Park, Benson & Fallding (1981) include a number that are probably fire-sensitive. These include Leucopogon amplexicaulis, found in areas with low fire frequency, L. margarodes in areas not burnt for eight to ten years, Darwinia procera on a rocky ridge, and D. glaucophylla on rock outcrops that evidently protect it from fire, but it is not known whether these have previously been more abundant and whether frequent burning has endangered them. 219 220 347 221 222 ## EE 223 224 # ——————————E—EEESEEEEeEE SSCS 225 226 Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 227 228 #### FIRE MANAGEMENT IN NATURAL AREAS 229 230 The effects of frequent burning in bushland areas have become particularly important with the increasing use of regular burning as a management tool. Such burning may be “controlled” (and intended only for fuel reduction) or “prescribed” (and sometimes involve biological as well as fuel reduction aims). Both involve the application of regular low-intensity fires, generally at intervals of between two and five years, though planned frequencies often vary widely in reality, to reduce flammable fuel. This is most commonly carried out during cool weather in autumn or spring, in order to keep fire intensities low and manageable. High-intensity prescribed burning is theoretically possible and may be biologically desirable, but there are problems with implementation (for details see Good, 1981, Luke & McArthur, 1978; Foster, 1976). 231 232 The use of control burning at these frequencies may have the following deleterious effects, which will be particularly undesirable in areas reserved for the protection of native plants. 233 234 (1) Fire-sensitive species may be eliminated by repeated burning at time intervals that are less than that required to produce seed. For example, burning an area several times in quick succession is reported by Luke & McArthur (1978) to eliminate species of Acacia by exhausting their seedbank without allowing it to be replaced. 235 236 (2) Fruiting in both fire-sensitive and fire-resistant species may be reduced by burning when the plants are in flower or have immature fruits. Though there will generally be some species in flower at any time of the year, many species have a concentrated peak in spring (Timms, 1978), followed by seed maturation and release in summer. This is common in the families Fabaceae and Rutaceae, which are particularly conspicuous in the Hawkesbury Sandstone flora. Thus, a season’s potential seed supply may be destroyed by burning when it is immature. 237 238 (3) Fire-resistant species may be eliminated by continual weakening and death of individuals. For example, Noble (1982) reports that in western New South Wales, mallee eucalypts, generally regarded as having a marked tolerance to periodic fire through their ability to produce epicormic shoots, do die when burnt more than once, especially when one burn closely follows another. 239 240 (4) Low-intensity fires may not stimulate adequate seedling germination, though allowing rhizomatous regeneration. Gill (1975) noted that for the Australian flora a high burning frequency often leads to dominance by monocotyledonous and fern species in place of shrubs. For example, Bradley (1972) reports on the occurrence of Pteridium esculentum and Culcita dubia after cool burns in Sydney bushland, while Luke & McArthur (1978) refer to /mperata cylindrica as prominent in coastal forests of northern New South Wales that have been burnt extensively. 241 242 A likely result of these factors is that areas of bush may be simplified both floristically and structurally. 243 244 For the fire-sensitive species examined, a period of six to seven years is needed to reach regular flowering. In addition, another year is required by some of the slowestflowering species to develop mature seed. The question of the time needed to establish adequate seedbank reserves, either in the soil or within the plant canopy, has not been determined for many species. It is likely that most species require several seed-bearing seasons for this. Thus, for the communities examined a minimum firefree period of nine to ten years is needed in a majority of fire cycles. An occasional burn followed quickly by another may be tolerated as seed reserves in the soil may 245 246 348 247 248 Cunninghamia 249 250 Vol. 1(3): 1985 251 252 not necessarily be exhausted by one fire. However, this is dependent on an adequate seedbank having been built up prior to the first fire. 253 254 The implications for fire management in natural areas are obvious. Before a long-term burning regime is imposed on an area of native bushland, the consequences of that action should be evaluated. As far as the survival of plant species is concerned, where there are often very little reliable data, it is necessary to err on the conservative side. That is, the time intervals between burns, in a majority of fire cycles, should be longer than the minimum suggested by the present findings. 255 256 ###### ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 257 258 This paper would not have been possible but for the enthusiasm and dedication of Dorothy Darvodelsky, Avril Donovan, Florence Dwight, Marie and John Glass, Marge Gowan, Valerie Jones, Clarice Morris and Peter Price, who germinated interest in the work and have continued with the data collection every three months, in all weathers. BENSON (Accepted for publication 11.5.1984) ABSTRACT Benson, D. H. (National Herbarium of New South Wales, Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia 2000) 1985. Maturation periods for fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation. Cunninghamia_1(3), 339-349, The maturation times (period from germination to flowering) for a number of fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation at sites in Brisbane Water National Park and at Glenorie near Sydney were recorded from marked seedlings established after hot fires. They range from two to seven years for different species. The implications for fire management, particularly for controlled burning, are discussed. A fire-{ree period of at least nine to ten years is recommended for similar vegetation if successful flowering and seed set, and continued species survival is to occur. ##### INTRODUCTION Plant species fall into two main groups with regard to their response to fire: some are characterized by vegetative regrowth, where individuals either resprout from epicormic shoots on the trunk and major surviving limbs or, following the death of all above-ground stems, resprout from underground rootstocks, lignotubers or rhizomes (sprouters); others regenerate from seed either stored in the soil before the fire, carried on the plants in woody fruits and released after the fire, or carried in from adjacent unburnt areas (non-sprouters). Adults in the second group are fire-sensitive and generally killed outright (Gill, 1975, 1981; Bradstock, 1981). The relative proportions of these groups of species appear to be related to the fire frequency in the habitat (Christensen, Recher & Hoare, 1981). In wet sclerophyll forest the proportion of fire-sensitive species is roughly 50 to 60 per cent (Ashton, 1981). In the more frequently burnt dry sclerophyll forests near Canberra, Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found 65 per cent regenerated vegetatively but only 27 per cent of species were fire-sensitive and only regenerated from seed. The time necessary for reproduction after fire is an important characteristic, especially in fire-sensitive species. Specht, Rayson & Jackman (1958) noted that fires at intervals of five years in heath vegetation are likely to eliminate or reduce numbers of some species that take several years to reach reproductive maturity. Similarly, for bushland north of Sydney, Siddiqi, Carolin & Myerscough (1976) recorded the localized elimination of the woody fire-sensitive species Banksia ericifolia, Allocasuarina distyla and Hakea teretifolia by repeated burning. However, to predict the impact of a series of fires, data on the maturation periods for fire-sensitive species are needed. With some exceptions, e.g. Banksia ericifolia (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) and Leptospermum laevigatum (Burrell, 1968), such data are not available. The potential effect of frequent burning on fire-sensitive species has become particularly relevant with the increased adoption of “controlled” or “prescribed” burning in bushland areas. Such burning generally involves the application of regular fires of low intensity, commonly at intervals of between two and five years. This paper documents the time required for a group of fire-sensitive species to reach maturity and discusses the implications for regular, frequent burning programs. 340 Cunninghamia Vol. 1{3): 1985 ##### METHODS The main study locality was in Brisbane Water National Park (33° 30'S, 151° 15'E), 40 km north of Sydney. Bushland here is eucalypt-dominated scleromorphic vegetation on low-nutrient Hawkesbury Sandstone. Rainfall is about 1250 mm per annum (Bureau of Meteorology, 1979). The general vegetation is described by Benson & Fallding (1981). A second locality was studied at Glenorie (33° 35’S, 151° 00'B), 15 km north-west of Hornsby, on similar Hawkesbury Sandstone, but with average rainfall of 930 mm per annum, to see whether similar results were obtained in a lower rainfall. A hot summer (1974-75) fire occurred at the Brisbane Water locality six months before the first observations were made and the size of dead bushes at the time indicated that the area had been unburnt for about 15 years before this. As a result of topographic and drainage features, there was considerable variation in microhabitat; therefore, four sites in generally similar, but slightly different, vegetation were chosen as follows: - Site A — low-woodland with Eucalyptus haemastoma and E. gummifera on a gently sloping hillside - Site B — open-heath on a broad rocky ledge - ® Site C — low open-forest of Banksia serrata and Eucalyptus gummifera ¢ Site D — woodland of Eucalyptus piperita subsp. piperita and E. gummifera on a - sandy ledge below a small cliff-line. A shrubby understorey characterized all the sites, although site C also had a considerable amount of grassy growth. Sites A and B were poorly drained. All sites were within about 0.5 km of each other. dry ridgetopThe Glenorieand hadsite wasbeen inburnt woodlandin Januaryof Eucalyptus1975, eximia and E. gummifera on a of At each site a transect of 10 contiguous 1m x 1m plots was established. Each these plots was subdivided into four 0.5m x 0.5 m sub-plots and two seedlings within each sub-plot were selected and marked with coloured wires. Seedlings were distinguished from plants regenerating from rootstocks or rhizomes by the presence of cotyledons or by comparison with similar plants that had been dug up and their roots examined. Although restricted to dicotyledonous species, as wide a range of species as possible was chosen, and the most healthy seedlings marked. Table | lists the 37 species included in this study, their susceptibility to fire and the total number of seedlings marked (“?” indicates species that are probably fire-sensitive). Initially, 320 seedlings were marked. Many of these died during the first years of recording. Additional plants were marked to replace dead plants during the first two years, after which no additional plants were marked. The occurrence of flowering was recorded four times a year (at Brisbane Water in early March, June, September and December; at Glenorie in early February, May, August and November) for the following eight years. At the same time all species flowering within about 30 m of the transect were recorded. Because of the range of microhabitats, such as minor cliff-lines, rock platforms and moist soaks, some of which remained unburnt during the fire, flowering recordings may represent as few as one or two individuals of a species, In July-August 1980 a low-intensity fire burnt part of the Brisbane Water area, including half of the site A transect. There was no canopy scorch and the fire was of Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 341 such low intensity that in places it was stopped by the trampled single-file track along the edge of the transect resulting from the three-monthly recordings. Although it reduced the amount of data from this site, a number of observations were made on species affected by the fire.
