lines: +Journal of the Royal Society of Western Australia, 91: 163-174, 2008
+# Post-fire juvenile period of plants in south-west Australia forests and implications for fire management
+N D Burrows¹, G Wardell-Johnson² & B Ward³
+¹ Department of Environment & Conservation, Locked Bag 104, Bentley Delivery Centre, WA 6983
+² Natural & Rural Systems Management, The University of Queensland, Gatton, Qld 4343
+³ Department of Environment & Conservation, Locked Bag 2, Manjimup, WA 6258
+Corresponding author: neilb@calm.wa.gov.au
+Manuscript received November 2007; accepted April 2008
+## Abstract

+Regular prescribed burning to manage the accumulation of flammable live and dead vegetation (fuel) is a strategy for ameliorating wildfire impacts in fire-prone environments. The interval between prescribed fires needs to be sufficient to manage fuel accumulation but it should also be ecologically acceptable. Time to first flowering after fire (juvenile period) is a biological indicator that can be used to guide minimum intervals between fires to conserve plant diversity. A survey of 639 plant species in forests and associated ecosystems of south-west Western Australian revealed that 97% of understorey species reached flowering age within 3 years of fire and all species reached flowering age within 5 years of fire. Within species variation was evident, with plants at the drier end of their range taking longer to reach flowering age. Fire sensitive plants, being obligate seeder species with longer juvenile periods (> 3 years), mostly occurred in low rainfall zones so took longer to mature, or in habitats that were less prone to fire because they remained moist for a longer period or because surface fuels were inherently sparse and discontinuous. Due to uncertainty about the reproductive biology and seed bank dynamics of most of the flora, we recommend that the conservative minimum interval between fires that are lethal to fire sensitive plants is about twice the juvenile period of the slowest maturing species in the community. Occasional landscape fires at shorter intervals would be ecologically acceptable only if these fires were of a sufficiently low intensity as to not kill plants with long juvenile periods, or were patchy and did not burn the habitats in which they occur.
+Keywords: fire, juvenile period, seeders, resprouters, prescribed burning
+## Introduction

+Plant communities in the south-west forest region of Western Australia display a remarkable array of physical and biological traits that enable them to persist in a fire prone environment, and in some cases depend upon fire for structural and floristic diversity (e.g., Gardner 1957, Christensen and Kimber 1975, Christensen and Abbott 1989 and Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). Fire regime is the history of fire frequency, season and intensity (Gill 1981) with fire frequency affecting both the structure of the vegetation and its floristic composition (Muir 1987, Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). Fire frequency also directly influences fire intensity because the quantity of live and dead vegetation, which becomes fuel for a bushfire, accumulates rapidly in the first 10 years after fire, after which the rate of fuel accumulation slows (Burrows 1994, McCaw et al. 1996).

+Today, intense summer wildfires threaten human life, destroy property and damage forest values such as timber and amenity. Large, intense wildfires can also be environmentally damaging and present a threat to ecosystem processes and conservation values including old growth forests, communities and species sensitive to high fire intensities, and extant populations of rare flora and fauna (see Abbott and Burrows 2003). Fire intensity, or the rate of heat energy release, is a measure of the severity of the fire; its damage potential, suppression difficulty and killing power. Wildfires derive their energy from the quantity and arrangement of live and dead vegetation (fuel) that burns. Fire intensity is further influenced by fuel dryness, weather conditions and topography. Of the factors that determine potential fire intensity, fuel quantity and weather conditions are the most influential, but fuel quantity is the only factor that can be effectively managed. Fuel reduction burning, the practise of purposefully setting low intensity fires under defined conditions of fuel, weather and topography, is a fire management technique to minimise the impact of wildfires by reducing the potential size and intensity of a wildfire, thereby reducing its damage potential and enhancing suppression opportunities. Prescribed burning does not prevent wildfires from occurring but where a significant proportion of the landscape is managed this

+way, wildfire impact can be considerably reduced. While there are few published cases where this practice has effectively reduced the impact of wildfires and contributed to suppression success (e.g. Rodger 1961, Underwood et al. 1985, Grant and Wouters 1993), there are numerous unpublished accounts by firefighters and land managers where prescribed burning has ameliorated wildfires (Cheney 1994). However, the practice of prescribed burning for fuel reduction is controversial with concerns that it is ecologically damaging in the long term.

+There have been many studies and observations of the ecological effects of a single fire on various plant species and communities in south-west ecosystems, however there are few published data on the long term ecological effects of repeated fuel reduction burning in south-west Australian forests (Christensen and Abbott 1989, Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). Burrows and Wardell-Johnson (2003) reported that 30 years of very frequent burning (3-4 year intervals) of an experimental site in a southern jarrah (*Eucalyptus marginata*) forest did not result in any species losses, but caused changes in the relative abundance of species over time including a decline in the abundance of two obligate seeder species and an increase in abundance of several other species. They also reported that none of the experimental fire regimes favoured all species, including long periods of fire exclusion. There was evidence that burning at 5-7 year intervals in spring and autumn caused no significant changes to species richness or abundance at the study site.

+In areas zoned for fuel reduction by prescribed burning, managers aim to maintain fine surface fuel quantity (dead leaves, twigs, bark and floral parts <6 mm in diameter) below about 8 t ha⁻¹ and 19 t ha⁻¹ for jarrah and karri (*E. diversicolor*) forests respectively. The higher fuel loading for karri reflects its more mesic, hence less flammable condition for a longer period throughout the year (McCaw and Hanstrum 2003). The time taken for fuels to reach these levels, hence the interval between prescribed fires, depends on the rate of fuel accumulation. This varies across the forest region from about 6 to 10 years, depending on site productivity and rainfall (Sneeuwjagt and Peet 1985, Burrows 1994). For example, in most jarrah forests, fine surface fuel quantity reaches quasi-equilibrium in 15-17 years (Burrows 1994).

+While about 70% of jarrah forest plant species have the capacity to resprout following fire, the remainder depend on seed (obligate seeders), stored either in the soil (soil-stored seeders) or in woody capsules in the canopy (canopy-stored seeders), for regeneration (Christensen and Kimber 1975, Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). An adequate viable seed store and conditions favourable for seed germination and plant growth are essential for flowering plants to persist in an ecosystem that is regularly burnt. For some species, fruit production and seed set may not occur in the first flowering year (Benson 1985, Wark et al. 1987, Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003) and seed production sufficient to provide adequate seed reserves to restore the population to pref-fire abundance levels may take many years (Gill and McMahon 1986, Gill and Nicholls 1989, Wooller et al. 2002). As observed by Gill and Nicholls (1989), seed production is the most relevant measure but flowering is a more practical measure. Gill and Nicholls (1989) suggest that doubling of the juvenile period of a species is a useful guide to when the species is likely to be able to replenish its seed bank following fire. This 'rule of thumb' is consistent with a number of individual species studies of seed production with time (see review by Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). However, there is a paucity of information about the reproductive biology and seed bank dynamics of plant species in Australian ecosystems (Whelan 1995, Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). Until more is known, knowing the juvenile period of species in an ecosystem subjected to regular fire is a useful criterion for determining the minimum fire interval between lethal fires and for assisting with defining ecologically sustainable fire regimes (Tolhurst 1999, Tolhurst 2004). If the interval between fires that are lethal to the parent plants is shorter than the time to first flowering (juvenile period) and seed set, then it is reasonable to assume that obligate seeder species especially, could be at risk of decline. However, if the intensity or patchiness of fires at short intervals is such that parent plants are not killed by fire, then populations may be able to persist and thrive under a regime of frequent but very low intensity, patchy fires.

+This paper reports on post-fire regeneration strategies, post-fire juvenile period and flowering phenology of 639 species that occur predominantly in the southern forests and associated ecosystems of south-west Western Australia. We also discuss how other factors such as climate (rainfall), regeneration strategy and life form influence age to first flowering.
+## Methods
+### Study sites

+Information about post-fire regeneration strategies, flowering time (month) and juvenile period (months) was gathered from study sites in the southern forest region of the south-west of Western Australia (Fig. 1). A brief description of each site is given in Table 1. The McCorkhill and Yendicup forest sites each comprised 10 small (each 4 ha) adjacent plots that were experimentally burnt at various times as part of a broader investigation into the long term effects of fire (see Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). The Lindsay forest site (Table 1) was similar except the plots were smaller (each about 0.5 ha). Data from the Walpole study site (Table 1) were accumulated from some 400 vegetation sample sites located throughout a broad range of vegetation types represented in the Walpole-Nornalup National Park (see Wardell-Johnson et al. 1989). Post-fire regeneration strategy and juvenile period were assessed at each site by regular (3-4 weekly) inspections until all species at the site had reached flowering age. The juvenile period is quite variable amongst individuals of the same species in the same population, so we define juvenile period as the time taken for at least 50% of individuals in a population to reach flowering age after fire. This was assessed visually. Visual inspection also ascertained the post-fire regeneration strategy, and plants were classified as shown in Table 2, which has been adapted from Gill (1981). +## Results

+Information on post-fire regeneration strategy, juvenile period and peak flowering month was documented for 639 plant species representing 249 genera and 72 families (Table 3). The most commonly observed families were Orchidaceae, Proteaceae, Papilionaceae, Myrtaceae, Epacridaceae, Asteraceae and Mimosaceae. The least commonly observed families included Portulaceae, Cephalotaceae, Lindsaeaceae, Zamiaceae, Loranthaceae, Podocarpaceae and Dennstaedtiaceae. At the intermediate and high rainfall sites (McCorkhill forest near Nannup, Lindsay forest near Manjimup and Walpole-Nornalup National Park), all upland forest understorey species reached flowering age within in 3 years of fire, with most (90%) flowering within 2 years (Fig. 2). At the lower rainfall site (Yendicup forest near Perup) all upland forest understorey species reached flowering age within 4 years of fire. Of the 639 species observed, 17 (3%) species had juvenile periods >3 years and three species were observed to take longer than 4 years to reach flowering after fire. +Intra-species variation in juvenile period was evident locally and regionally with plants growing in the lower rainfall areas often taking considerably longer to flower than the same species at higher rainfall sites. Some examples are shown in Table 5.

+Mean juvenile period, or secondary juvenile period in the case of resprouters (Gill 1975), for various plant life forms is shown in Table 6. As to be expected, trees, lower trees and woody shrubs took longer to flower after fire than geophytes, grasses and annual herbs. All overstorey tree species (*Eucalyptus* spp.) and many lower tree species (e.g. some *Banksia* spp.) were capable of both re-sprouting and regenerating from seed after fire; the juvenile period reported here is for mature plants that have re-sprouted. The juvenile period of plants regenerating from seed would be considerably longer (probably 10-20 years for eucalypts). There was a statistically significant difference (á = 0.05) in juvenile period between seeders and resprouters in almost all life form categories with resprouters flowering sooner than obligate seeders, the exception being grasses, where seeders flowered sooner. Mean juvenile period for plants in each of the nine post-fire regeneration categories is shown in Figure 3. Overall, canopy-stored seeders had the longest juvenile period (mean about 36 months) and geophytes (especially Orchidaceae, Droseraceae) and plants with large apical buds (Xanthorroeaceae and Dasypogonaceae) took the shortest time to flower (mean about 10 months). *Kingia australis* (Dasypogonaceae) had the shortest juvenile period with most of the population flowering within 2 months of fire; plants with stems shorter than about 100 cm had few or no flowers, suggesting they had not reached reproductive maturity.

Of the 639 species observed in this study, 619 (~97%) reached flowering age within three years of fire, and all species had flowered within 5 years of fire. While this sample (639) is about a quarter of the known flora of the region, it represents a cross-section of habitat types, life forms and of taxa. This relatively rapid post-fire growth and maturation (short juvenile period) is not surprising given these ecosystems have a very long association with fire. Understorey species with juvenile periods longer than 3 years were confined to either the less productive lower rainfall zones of the forest region or to less flammable habitat elements in the landscape. The importance of climate (especially rainfall) in influencing juvenile period is further evidenced by the intra-specific variation shown in Table 5. Habitat flammability is broadly determined by the seasonal rhythm of moisture regime (McCaw and Hanstrum 2003) or by the quantity, structure and continuity of the vegetation complex, which becomes fuel for a bushfire. Parts of the landscape that stay moist for longer periods, such as some riparian zones, valley floors and swamp complexes, have a shorter period of the year when live and dead vegetation (fuel) is sufficiently dry to sustain fire, therefore a lower probability of combusting, so it is not surprising that species with longer juvenile periods most often occur in these areas. Other flat or low-lying, moisture gaining parts of the landscape, such as some myrtaceous swamps, are highly flammable for long periods of the year because of greater exposure to wind and solar radiation and because of the nature, structure and quantity of the elevated vegetation. However, it is unusual to find species with long juvenile periods in these habitats. Habitats with low or discontinuous fuels (such as rock outcrops and some swamp and woodland complexes) usually only carry fire under dry and windy conditions, further limiting the time throughout the year when conditions are such that these areas can burn. Thus, and as to be expected, understorey species with longer juvenile periods (>3 years) occur in habitats that are less prone to fire and are commonly tall shrubs and lower tree species such as *Banksia* spp. (Table 4). On the other hand, plants with long juvenile periods are rarely found in parts of the landscape that are more prone to fire because these habitats are drier for longer periods and support continuous surface fuels, such as forested plateaus and uplands (see Table 4). Clarke (2002) working in south-east Australian forest ecosystems reported that rock outcrops and pavements were dissimilar in species composition from the surrounding forest and were dominated by shrubs that were readily killed by fire and depended on post-fire seedling recruitment. In contrast, the most abundant species in the adjacent, more flammable forest, were post-fire resprouters.

+Muir (1987) found that of the 198 plant species he observed throughout the south-west, mid-west, wheatbelt, south coast and goldfields regions of Western Australia, almost 74% flowered within 4 years of fire, but about 26% took 5-8 years to flower. Of the species that took 5-8 years to flower, 7 (13%) occurred in the forest region, the remainder occurring in the lower rainfall areas outside the forest region. Of these, four are resprouters (*Agonis flexuosa*, *Astartea fascicularis*, *Banksia grandis* and *Regelia ciliata*), which we recorded flowering 24-36 months after fire, and the remainder (*Casuarina obesa*, *Melaleuca diosmifolia* and *M. laterita*) occur in or around swamps or winter-wet depressions. Van der Moezel et al. (1987) documented the juvenile period of 192 species of the northern sandplain kwongan near Badgingarra (mean annual rainfall about 500 mm) and reported that 79% of species flowered within 2 years of fire, with all species observed flowering within 5 years of fire. These data support the proposition that mean annual rainfall and spatial and temporal variability in landscape flammability are significant factors influencing the distribution of fire regime sensitive plant species, which are mostly obligate seeder species with relatively long juvenile periods.

+Fine surface fuel (dead leaves, twigs, bark, fruits) on the forest floor provides the dominant fuel layer because of its position (at the base of the fuel ladder), quantity and continuity (Burrows 1994). Forest fires are unlikely to spread when the surface fuel moisture content exceeds about 21% or when the surface fuel quantity is below about 4 t ha⁻¹ (Burrows 1994). Under extreme fire weather conditions, which are likely to occur on only 1-2 days each year (McCaw and Hanstrum 2003), fire spread may be sustained when the surface fuel quantity is as low as 3 t ha⁻¹ but fires are generally low intensity and patchy. +Journal of the Royal Society of Western Australia, 91(2), June 2008
+[Line graph: fine surface fuel (t ha⁻¹) against time since fire (yrs) 0-10; high rainfall and low rainfall curves, fuel upper limit and fire spread threshold lines]

+## Management implications

+Prescribed burning for fuel management in jarrah forests aims to maintain fine surface fuel quantities in strategic areas below about 8 t ha⁻¹ (McCaw and Burrows 1989). Burrows et al.: Post-fire juvenile period of plants in SW Australia

burning can be planned and implemented under seasonal and diurnal weather conditions to exploit these temporal and spatial flammability differentials, thereby reducing the risk of burning fire sensitive species and communities too frequently. In south-west forest landscapes, low intensity prescribed fires set under moist conditions in spring usually burn the drier parts of the landscape, such as forested uplands, but often do not burn riparian zones and areas of sparse fine surface fuels such as rock outcrops. The proportion of the landscape that is sufficiently dry to burn increases rapidly with the onset of summer drying and where fuels are continuous, fires in summer and autumn usually burn the entire landscape.

## Conclusion

Juvenile period can be used as a biological indicator to help determine ecologically acceptable minimum intervals between fires in various ecosystems. The post-fire juvenile period of understorey plants in south-west forests and associated ecosystems reflects site productivity, as expressed by rainfall, and habitat flammability, as determined by seasonal moisture regime and fuel characteristics. Plants with longer juvenile periods are most likely to occur in the lower rainfall regions, and in less flammable habitats such as riparian zones, rock outcrops and some wetlands. At the landscape scale, the minimum ecologically acceptable fire interval will vary across the landscape in response to changing habitat types. In the interests of plant conservation, fire management, particularly the interval between prescribed fires, should aim to accommodate this variability.

+Burrows et al.: Post-fire juvenile period of plants in SW Australia

+burning can be planned and implemented under seasonal and diurnal weather conditions to exploit these temporal and spatial flammability differentials, thereby reducing the risk of burning fire sensitive species and communities too frequently. In south-west forest landscapes, low intensity prescribed fires set under moist conditions in spring usually burn the drier parts of the landscape, such as forested uplands, but often do not burn riparian zones and areas of sparse fine surface fuels such as rock outcrops. The proportion of the landscape that is sufficiently dry to burn increases rapidly with the onset of summer drying and where fuels are continuous, fires in summer and autumn usually burn the entire landscape.
+## Conclusion

+Juvenile period can be used as a biological indicator to help determine ecologically acceptable minimum intervals between fires in various ecosystems. The post-fire juvenile period of understorey plants in south-west forests and associated ecosystems reflects site productivity, as expressed by rainfall, and habitat flammability, as determined by seasonal moisture regime and fuel characteristics. Plants with longer juvenile periods are most likely to occur in the lower rainfall regions, and in less flammable habitats such as riparian zones, rock outcrops and some wetlands. At the landscape scale, the minimum ecologically acceptable fire interval will vary across the landscape in response to changing habitat types. In the interests of plant conservation, fire management, particularly the interval between prescribed fires, should aim to accommodate this variability.

+Acknowledgements - We thank Tony Annels, Chris Vellios, Alex Robinson and Ian Wheeler (Department of Conservation and Land Management, Manjimup Western Australia) for their assistance in the field and the Western Australian Herbarium for assisting with plant identification and specimen vouchering.

-# Post-fire juvenile period of plants in south-west Australia forests and implications for fire management
-N D Burrows!, G Wardell-Johnson’ & B Ward?

-1 Department of Environment & Conservation, Locked Bag 104, Bentley Delivery Centre, WA 6983 ? Natural & Rural Systems Management, The University of Queensland, Gatton, Qld 4343 2 Department of Environment & Conservation, Locked Bag 2, Manjimup, WA 6258 Corresponding author: Dd neilb@calm.wa.gov.au
-Manuscript received November 2007; accepted April 2008
-#### Abstract

-Regular prescribed burning to manage the accumulation of flammable live and dead vegetation (fuel) is a strategy for ameliorating wildfire impacts in fire-prone environments. The interval between prescribed fires needs to be sufficient to manage fuel accumulation but it should also be ecologically acceptable. Time to first flowering after fire (juvenile period) is a biological indicator that can be used to guide minimum intervals between fires to conserve plant diversity. A survey of 639 plant species in forests and associated ecosystems of south-west Western Australian revealed that 97% of understorey species reached flowering age within 3 years of fire and all species reached flowering age within 5 years of fire. Within species variation was evident, with plants at the drier end of their range taking longer to reach flowering age. Fire sensitive plants, being obligate seeder species with longer juvenile periods (> 3 years), mostly occurred in low rainfall zones so took longer to mature, or in habitats that were léss prone to fire because they remained moist for a longer period or because surface fuels were inherently sparse and discontinuous. Due to uncertainty about the reproductive biology and seed bank dynamics of most of the flora, we recommend that the conservative minimum interval between fires that are lethal to fire sensitive plants is about twice the juvenile period of the slowest maturing species in the community. Occasional landscape fires at shorter intervals would be ecologically acceptable only if these fires were of a sufficiently low intensity as to not kill plants with long juvenile periods, or were patchy and did not burn the habitats in which they occur.
-Keywords: fire, juvenile period, seeders, resprouters, prescribed burning

Burrows et al.: Post-fire juvenile period of plants in SW Australia

burning can be planned and implemented under seasonal and diurnal weather conditions to exploit these temporal and spatial flammability differentials, thereby reducing the risk of burning fire sensitive species and communities too frequently. In south-west forest landscapes, low intensity prescribed fires set under moist conditions in spring usually burn the drier parts of the landscape, such as forested uplands, but often do not burn riparian zones and areas of sparse fine surface fuels such as rock outcrops. The proportion of the landscape that is sufficiently dry to burn increases rapidly with the onset of summer drying and where fuels are continuous, fires in summer and autumn usually burn the entire landscape.

## Conclusion

Juvenile period can be used as a biological indicator to help determine ecologically acceptable minimum intervals between fires in various ecosystems. The post-fire juvenile period of understorey plants in south-west forests and associated ecosystems reflects site productivity, as expressed by rainfall, and habitat flammability, as determined by seasonal moisture regime and fuel characteristics. Plants with longer juvenile periods are most likely to occur in the lower rainfall regions, and in less flammable habitats such as riparian zones, rock outcrops and some wetlands. At the landscape scale, the minimum ecologically acceptable fire interval will vary across the landscape in response to changing habitat types. In the interests of plant conservation, fire management, particularly the interval between prescribed fires, should aim to accommodate this variability.

content.content:
=== PAGE 2
Journal of
Ecology 1996,
84, 9-17

© 1996 British
Ecological Society

Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for
the highly serotinous shrub, Banksia hookeriana

N.J. ENRIGHT,** BYRON B. LAMONT# and RALF MARSULAt

*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia,

+ School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and
tSektion Okosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2,

0-7050 Leipzig, Germany

Summary

1 Banksia hookeriana is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone
northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire
frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed
demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field
data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy
was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles,
holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated
widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an
estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1—10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture
(i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles
remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after
10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued
to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at
least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been
lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
6 Shannon—Weiner diversity (H’) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with
plant age, while evenness (V’) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then
increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of
individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18
years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be
minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the
natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

Keywords: Banksia, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

Journal of Ecology (1996) 84, 9-17

Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits
within the plant canopy for more than one year, and
can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds:

Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of
Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Mel-
bourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 393444972, E-
mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au

storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived
seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al.
1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally
triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release,
germinating during the first favourable period (Cow-
ling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly
serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few
years of production, to strongly serotinous, where
seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

=== PAGE 3
10

Canopy seed bank
dynamics in
Banksia
hookeriana

© 1996 British
Ecological Society,
Journal of Ecology,
84, 9-17

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where
conditions for seedling recruitment are best immedi-
ately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture
and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued
release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the
age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the popu-
lation by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that
establish later during the interfire period have a low
probability of survival due to competition with their
parents and other established plants (Cowling &
Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be
much younger and, on average, will have a smaller
canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit
(sensu Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss
in relation to plant age determines the range of fire
frequencies for which population maintenance is
possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of
reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy
seed bank has accumulated, then a population is
threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by
the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the like-
lihood of plant recruitment and survival to repro-
ductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened
by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and
plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means
that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost
where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate
not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds
may survive for many years after the death of parent
plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is
more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the
canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely
to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

Banksia hookeriana Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a
highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody
shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern
sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia
about 250-330km north of Perth (George 1981;
Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of
enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large
infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new
inflorescences may be damaged and removed from
plants by birds, mature cones normally remain
attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds
abort during development, while others are either
released gradually or (especially after fire) are con-
sumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain
viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset
of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil
seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 x 30km) of the low
nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the dis-
tribution of this species, which is further limited by
its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune
crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989).
This means that the species exists as a large number
of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100

to > 10000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2
to > 1km. The largest populations are located near
Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range.
Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral
exploration, and increased incidence of anthro-
pogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire
frequency potential threats to the long term survival
of this species. In addition, its attractive orange
inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the
commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed pro-
duction in exploited populations (Witkowski et al.
1994),

This paper describes seed production and avail-
ability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics
in Banksia hookeriana in relation to plant age (= time
since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following
questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant
age, and what factors influence the rate of seed
accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny,
granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the
optimum fire frequency to which the species is
adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible
with population survival?

STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature
Reserve about 330km north of Perth (29°25’S,

within the plant canopy for more than one year, and
can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds:

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where
conditions for seedling recruitment are best immedi-

and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued
release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the
age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the popu-
lation by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that
establish later during the interfire period have a low
probability of survival due to competition with their
parents and other established plants (Cowling &
Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be
much younger and, on average, will have a smaller
canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit
(sensu Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss
in relation to plant age determines the range of fire
frequencies for which population maintenance is
possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of
reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy
seed bank has accumulated, then a population is
threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by
the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the like-
lihood of plant recruitment and survival to repro-
ductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened
by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and
plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means
that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost

not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds
may survive for many years after the death of parent
plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is
more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the
canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely
to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

Banksia hookeriana Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a
highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody

sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia

closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of
spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c,

Since plants only began to set viable seed at an
age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle
rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there
was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in
plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the per-
centage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all fol-

established in the sample plots as a result of interfire
seed release survived for more than one year.

attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay

Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was con-
centrated on new cones since the largely host-specific
insect larvae which eat Banksia seeds can only tunnel
through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He
argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with
age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vul-
nerable to invasion. However, Cowling et al. (1987)
concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred
in older cones for Banksia menziesii and Banksia
prionotes. A similar finding was obtained here for
Banksia hookeriana (Table 1): While granivory was
greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at
arate of 2-3% of follicles per year in cones of increas-
ing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded
granivory in old cones of Banksia ericifolia at Ku-
ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but
suggested that the trend might be explained by higher
rates of infestation in the first few years of seed pro-
duction when fewer inflorescences were available.
However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from
young stands provided only limited support for this
explanation.

SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY

According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to
fire per se, but to a particular fire regime. The number
of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants
may largely determine the number offspring left after
a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable
seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases,
and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle
opening, granivory and decay might appropriately
describe the optimum life history strategy for a non-
sprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The
canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these
patterns of accumulation and loss.

Early in the reproductive life of individuals of
Banksia hookeriana (5-8 years of age) few viable seeds
are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number
of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small
and there is a low likelihood of successful parent
replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling
mortality typical of the first few years following fire
(Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on
seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert
National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) esti-
mated that parent replacement in Banksia ornata
populations was unlikely until plants held ~ 100
viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant
age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on
recruitment of Banksia hookeriana near Mt Adams
following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in
1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were
released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age
of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is
assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent
replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire

interval for Banksia hookeriana plants would be at
least 8 years.

The total number of viable seeds lost from the
canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly
with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the
excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant’s
lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As
plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total
losses approached and finally exceeded the number of
viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to
occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.

Using the simplifying assumption that self-replace-
ment, on average, required release of at least 100
viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the
finite rate of natural increase (A) can be calculated for
each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum
value of 2 assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (A
as a measure of fitness, sensu Stearns 1992). Popu-
lations of Banksia hookeriana near Mt Adams appear
optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16-17 years
(Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the
number of viable seeds released after fire relative to
the total investment of energy and nutrients expended
on seed production. Although the size of the canopy
seed bank continued to grow until plants were about
25 years old, predicted A decreased as plant age
increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly
more resources are wasted on seeds which perish dur-
ing the interfire period through spontaneous release
into a highly competitive environment where suc-
cessful recruitment is unlikely, and through pre-
dispersal granivory and decay.

However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is
dependent upon the estimated number of seeds
needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate
is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed)
then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

(less likelihood of recruitment) the optimum occurs
later. It is likely that the true value varies from fire to
fire, reflecting differences in the suitability of weather
conditions for postfire recruitment (Enright &
Lamont 1992a,b). For estimates ranging from half
(50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds
required per parent (relative to that used above), the
optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years,
respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.

If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years,
opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase
due to the release of sites within stands resulting from
death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) docu-
ments the decline of serotinous Proteaceae popu-
lations in South African fynbos which have remained
unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no
successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in
Banksia hookeriana for stands up to 21 years old. The
lack of older sites precludes further direct study of
this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e.
seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply
that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire
recurs. In support of this contention, we have been
unable to locate any sites containing plants older than
23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). How-
ever, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire
frequency due to human interference.

Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store
modelled here had not peaked by the estimated opti-
mum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H’)
rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and
evenness is always high. One possible consequence of
dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced
in different years which might reflect different pollen
parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it
increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might
help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary
drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the
species in the face of fluctuating environmental con-
ditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species
characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants
represent different generations. The advantages for
longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as Bank-
sia hookeriana are less obvious, as all or most pollen
will derive from neighbours of identical age which
were recruited following the same disturbance and
have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead,
selfing would probably increase with age as flower
head production per plant and death of neighbours
increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity.
Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting
species (such as Banksia hookeriana) are prone to
strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling
stage. He considered that the high number of discrete
sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations
through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid
evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of
speciation in Banksia and other taxa with similar life
histories.

The recent history of fire within the geographical
range of Banksia hookeriana suggests shorter intervals
between successive fires than we propose as optimal
for species’ maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984
burned 117000ha of the northern sandplain heath
(van der Moezel et al. 1987), an area equivalent to
nearly half of the total geographical range of the spec-
ies. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part
of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period
of only 7 years. This fire eliminated Banksia hook-
eriana from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der
Moezel et al. (1987) comment that areas of sandplain
heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming
increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms
and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning
policy for the remaining natural vegetation.

Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was con-
centrated on new cones since the largely host-specific
insect larvae which eat Banksia seeds can only tunnel
through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He
argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with
age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vul-
nerable to invasion. However, Cowling et al. (1987)
concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred
in older cones for Banksia menziesii and Banksia
prionotes. A similar finding was obtained here for
Banksia hookeriana (Table 1): While granivory was
greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at
arate of 2-3% of follicles per year in cones of increas-
ing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded
granivory in old cones of Banksia ericifolia at Ku-
ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but
suggested that the trend might be explained by higher
rates of infestation in the first few years of seed pro-
duction when fewer inflorescences were available.
However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from
young stands provided only limited support for this
explanation.

SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY

According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to
fire per se, but to a particular fire regime. The number
of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants
may largely determine the number offspring left after
a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable
seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases,
and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle
opening, granivory and decay might appropriately
describe the optimum life history strategy for a non-
sprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The
canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these
patterns of accumulation and loss.

Early in the reproductive life of individuals of
Banksia hookeriana (5-8 years of age) few viable seeds
are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number
of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small
and there is a low likelihood of successful parent
replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling
mortality typical of the first few years following fire
(Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on
seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert
National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) esti-
mated that parent replacement in Banksia ornata
populations was unlikely until plants held ~ 100
viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant
age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on
recruitment of Banksia hookeriana near Mt Adams
following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in
1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were
released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age
of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is
assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent
replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire

interval for Banksia hookeriana plants would be at
least 8 years.

The total number of viable seeds lost from the
canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly
with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the
excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant’s
lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As
plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total
losses approached and finally exceeded the number of
viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to
occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.

Using the simplifying assumption that self-replace-
ment, on average, required release of at least 100
viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the
finite rate of natural increase (A) can be calculated for
each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum
value of 2 assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (A
as a measure of fitness, sensu Stearns 1992). Popu-
lations of Banksia hookeriana near Mt Adams appear
optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16-17 years
(Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the
number of viable seeds released after fire relative to
the total investment of energy and nutrients expended
on seed production. Although the size of the canopy
seed bank continued to grow until plants were about
25 years old, predicted A decreased as plant age
increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly
more resources are wasted on seeds which perish dur-
ing the interfire period through spontaneous release
into a highly competitive environment where suc-
cessful recruitment is unlikely, and through pre-
dispersal granivory and decay.

However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is
dependent upon the estimated number of seeds
needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate
is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed)
then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

(50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds
required per parent (relative to that used above), the
optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years,
respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.

If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years,
opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase
due to the release of sites within stands resulting from
death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) docu-
ments the decline of serotinous Proteaceae popu-
lations in South African fynbos which have remained
unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no
successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in
Banksia hookeriana for stands up to 21 years old. The
lack of older sites precludes further direct study of
this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e.
seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply
that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire
recurs. In support of this contention, we have been
unable to locate any sites containing plants older than
23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). How-
ever, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire
frequency due to human interference.

Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store
modelled here had not peaked by the estimated opti-
mum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H’)
rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and
evenness is always high. One possible consequence of
dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced
in different years which might reflect different pollen
parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it
increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might
help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary
drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the
species in the face of fluctuating environmental con-
ditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species
characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants
represent different generations. The advantages for
longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as Bank-
sia hookeriana are less obvious, as all or most pollen
will derive from neighbours of identical age which
were recruited following the same disturbance and
have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead,
selfing would probably increase with age as flower
head production per plant and death of neighbours
increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity.
Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting
species (such as Banksia hookeriana) are prone to
strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling
stage. He considered that the high number of discrete
sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations
through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid
evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of
speciation in Banksia and other taxa with similar life
histories.

The recent history of fire within the geographical
range of Banksia hookeriana suggests shorter intervals
between successive fires than we propose as optimal
for species’ maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984
burned 117000ha of the northern sandplain heath
(van der Moezel et al. 1987), an area equivalent to
nearly half of the total geographical range of the spec-
ies. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part
of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period
of only 7 years. This fire eliminated Banksia hook-
eriana from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der
Moezel et al. (1987) comment that areas of sandplain
heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming
increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms
and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning
policy for the remaining natural vegetation.

# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany

## Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17

## Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 393444972, E-mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au

© 1996 British Ecological Society

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski *et al.* 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont *et al.* 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski *et al.* 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

### STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

## Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m² in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m² subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).

For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.

Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling *et al.* 1987).

### STATISTICAL ANALYSES

Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.

A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) and evenness (V′) were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.

## Results

### CONE PRODUCTION

A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.

The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).

### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE

In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10–12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.

Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.

The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.

Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).

### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL

By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.

The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples

Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.

Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages represented in the canopy seed bank increased continuously with plant age following the onset of reproductive maturity; quickly at first as the number of seed ages represented increased on young plants (H′ = 0.66 at 6 years, to H′ = 2.00 at 15 years), and then more slowly as the number of seed ages represented on the plant stabilised (H′ = 2.28 at 25 years). The continued increase in H′ after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V′) of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V′ = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V′ = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V′ = 0.88 at 25 years).

## Discussion

### SEED DEMOGRAPHY

Flowering in *Banksia hookeriana* commenced at an age of 3-4 years, but few or no viable seeds were stored on plants <5 years old, so that recurrent fire within this time would lead to loss of the species from the community. The time to first reproduction is similar to that described for a number of other serotinous, nonsprouting trees and shrubs in southern and eastern Australian scrub-heaths (Bradstock 1985;

Despite large year to year variations in cone production, on average the total number of cones in the crown showed a steady increase with age. McMaster & Zedler (1981), Lamont *et al.* (1991a), and others hypothesized that canopy seed storage (serotiny) may dampen annual fluctuations in production, ensuring adequate seed supply following fire. The present results support this contention: seeds produced in years of high seed production were nearly all held on the plant for at least 5 years so that years of low seed production did not impact in the short term on the total canopy seed store.

Cowling *et al.* (1987) found that years of high seed production were associated with low rates of predispersal granivory by insects, implying satiation of granivores. If serotiny dampens fluctuations in seed availability, as suggested above, then these year to year variations would not prove effective in limiting the impacts of insect granivores unless granivory were

restricted to follicles on cones less than one year old. Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was concentrated on new cones since the largely host-specific insect larvae which eat *Banksia* seeds can only tunnel through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vulnerable to invasion. However, Cowling *et al.* (1987) concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred in older cones for *Banksia menziesii* and *Banksia prionotes*. A similar finding was obtained here for *Banksia hookeriana* (Table 1): While granivory was greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at a rate of 2–3% of follicles per year in cones of increasing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded granivory in old cones of *Banksia ericifolia* at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but suggested that the trend might be explained by higher rates of infestation in the first few years of seed production when fewer inflorescences were available. However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from young stands provided only limited support for this explanation.

### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY

According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a nonsprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.

Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5–8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire interval for *Banksia hookeriana* plants would be at least 8 years.

The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.

Using the simplifying assumption that self-replacement, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, *sensu* Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16–17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly more resources are wasted on seeds which perish during the interfire period through spontaneous release into a highly competitive environment where successful recruitment is unlikely, and through predispersal granivory and decay.

However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is dependent upon the estimated number of seeds needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed) then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased
